cards.back: Cellulose occurs exclusively in plants and it is the most abundant organic substance in plant kingdom.
cards.quote: Cellulose occurs exclusively in plants and it is the most abundant organic substance in plant kingdom.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Of what is cellulose a predominant constituent?
cards.back: cell wall of plant cells
cards.quote: It is a predominant constituent of cell wall of plant cells.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In what form are carbohydrates stored in the animal body?
cards.back: glycogen
cards.quote: The carbohydrates are stored in animal body as glycogen.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is glycogen also known as animal starch?
cards.back: It is also known as animal starch because its structure is similar to amylopectin and is rather more highly branched.
cards.quote: It is also known as animal starch because its structure is similar to amylopectin and is rather more highly branched.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Where is glycogen present in the animal body?
cards.back: It is present in liver, muscles and brain.
cards.quote: It is present in liver, muscles and brain.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What happens to glycogen when the body needs glucose?
cards.back: When the body needs glucose, enzymes break the glycogen down to glucose.
cards.quote: When the body needs glucose, enzymes break the glycogen down to glucose.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Besides the animal body, where is glycogen also found?
cards.back: yeast and fungi
cards.quote: Glycogen is also found in yeast and fungi.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which carbohydrates are used as storage molecules in plants and in animals?
cards.back: Carbohydrates are used as storage molecules as starch in plants and glycogen in animals.
cards.quote: Carbohydrates are used as storage molecules as starch in plants and glycogen in animals.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which two aldopentoses are present in nucleic acids?
cards.back: Two aldopentoses viz. D-ribose and 2-deoxy-D-ribose (Section 10.5.1, Class XII) are present in nucleic acids.
cards.quote: Two aldopentoses viz. D-ribose and 2-deoxy-D-ribose (Section 10.5.1, Class XII) are present in nucleic acids.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Carbohydrates provide raw materials for which important industries?
cards.back: textiles, paper, lacquers and breweries
cards.quote: They provide raw materials for many important industries like textiles, paper, lacquers and breweries.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which biomolecules are the most abundant in the living system?
cards.back: Proteins
cards.quote: Proteins are the most abundant biomolecules of the living system.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which functional groups do amino acids contain?
cards.back: Amino acids contain amino (–NH2) and carboxyl (–COOH) functional groups.
cards.quote: Amino acids contain amino (–NH2) and carboxyl (–COOH) functional groups.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Amino acids are classified into which three kinds?
cards.back:
acidic
basic
neutral
cards.quote: Amino acids are classified as acidic, basic or neutral depending upon the relative number of amino and carboxyl groups in their molecule.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: When is an amino acid neutral, basic or acidic?
cards.back: Equal number of amino and carboxyl groups makes it neutral; more number of amino than carboxyl groups makes it basic and more carboxyl groups as compared to amino groups makes it acidic.
cards.quote: Equal number of amino and carboxyl groups makes it neutral; more number of amino than carboxyl groups makes it basic and more carboxyl groups as compared to amino groups makes it acidic.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are non-essential amino acids?
cards.back: The amino acids, which can be synthesised in the body, are known as non-essential amino acids.
cards.quote: The amino acids, which can be synthesised in the body, are known as non-essential amino acids.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are essential amino acids?
cards.back: those which cannot be synthesised in the body and must be obtained through diet, are known as essential amino acids
cards.quote: those which cannot be synthesised in the body and must be obtained through diet, are known as essential amino acids

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How many amino acids are called essential amino acids, and why?
cards.back: Ten amino acids are called essential amino acids because they cannot be synthesised by our body, hence must be provided through diet.
cards.quote: Ten amino acids are called essential amino acids because they cannot be synthesised by our body, hence must be provided through diet.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are the usual physical properties of amino acids?
cards.back: Amino acids are usually colourless, crystalline solids. These are water-soluble, high melting solids and behave like salts rather than simple amines or carboxylic acids.
cards.quote: Amino acids are usually colourless, crystalline solids. These are water-soluble, high melting solids and behave like salts rather than simple amines or carboxylic acids.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why do amino acids behave like salts rather than simple amines or carboxylic acids?
cards.back: This behaviour is due to the presence of both acidic (carboxyl group) and basic (amino group) groups in the same molecule.
cards.quote: This behaviour is due to the presence of both acidic (carboxyl group) and basic (amino group) groups in the same molecule.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a zwitter ion?
cards.back: In aqueous solution, the carboxyl group can lose a proton and amino group can accept a proton, giving rise to a dipolar ion known as zwitter ion. This is neutral but contains both positive and negative charges.
cards.quote: In aqueous solution, the carboxyl group can lose a proton and amino group can accept a proton, giving rise to a dipolar ion known as zwitter ion. This is neutral but contains both positive and negative charges.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why do amino acids show amphoteric behaviour?
cards.back: In zwitter ionic form, amino acids show amphoteric behaviour as they react both with acids and bases.
cards.quote: In zwitter ionic form, amino acids show amphoteric behaviour as they react both with acids and bases.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which configuration do most naturally occurring amino acids have, and how is it written?
cards.back: Most naturally occurring amino acids have L-configuration. L-Aminoacids are represented by writing the –NH2 group on left hand side.
cards.quote: Most naturally occurring amino acids have L-configuration. L-Aminoacids are represented by writing the –NH2 group on left hand side.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a peptide linkage, chemically?
cards.back: Chemically, peptide linkage is an amide formed between –COOH group and –NH2 group.
cards.quote: Chemically, peptide linkage is an amide formed between –COOH group and –NH2 group.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is eliminated when two amino acids join, and what bond forms?
cards.back: This results in the elimination of a water molecule and formation of a peptide bond –CO–NH–.
cards.quote: This results in the elimination of a water molecule and formation of a peptide bond –CO–NH–.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the product of two amino acids joining by a peptide bond called?
cards.back: a dipeptide
cards.quote: The product of the reaction is called a dipeptide because it is made up of two amino acids.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a tripeptide?
cards.back: If a third amino acid combines to a dipeptide, the product is called a tripeptide. A tripeptide contains three amino acids linked by two peptide linkages.
cards.quote: If a third amino acid combines to a dipeptide, the product is called a tripeptide. A tripeptide contains three amino acids linked by two peptide linkages.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Names of the products when four, five or six amino acids are linked
cards.back:
tetrapeptide
pentapeptide
hexapeptide
cards.quote: when four, five or six amino acids are linked, the respective products are known as tetrapeptide, pentapeptide or hexapeptide, respectively.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are polypeptides?
cards.back: When the number of such amino acids is more than ten, then the products are called polypeptides.
cards.quote: When the number of such amino acids is more than ten, then the products are called polypeptides.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: When is a polypeptide called a protein?
cards.back: A polypeptide with more than hundred amino acid residues, having molecular mass higher than 10,000u is called a protein.
cards.quote: A polypeptide with more than hundred amino acid residues, having molecular mass higher than 10,000u is called a protein.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How many amino acids does insulin contain?
cards.back: Polypeptides with fewer amino acids are likely to be called proteins if they ordinarily have a well defined conformation of a protein such as insulin which contains 51 amino acids.
cards.quote: Polypeptides with fewer amino acids are likely to be called proteins if they ordinarily have a well defined conformation of a protein such as insulin which contains 51 amino acids.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are fibrous proteins?
cards.back: When the polypeptide chains run parallel and are held together by hydrogen and disulphide bonds, then fibre-like structure is formed. Such proteins are generally insoluble in water.
cards.quote: When the polypeptide chains run parallel and are held together by hydrogen and disulphide bonds, then fibre-like structure is formed. Such proteins are generally insoluble in water.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name two fibrous proteins and where each is present.
cards.back: Some common examples are keratin (present in hair, wool, silk) and myosin (present in muscles), etc.
cards.quote: Some common examples are keratin (present in hair, wool, silk) and myosin (present in muscles), etc.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are globular proteins?
cards.back: This structure results when the chains of polypeptides coil around to give a spherical shape. These are usually soluble in water.
cards.quote: This structure results when the chains of polypeptides coil around to give a spherical shape. These are usually soluble in water.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name common examples of globular proteins.
cards.back: Insulin and albumins
cards.quote: Insulin and albumins are the common examples of globular proteins.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: At which four levels can the structure and shape of proteins be studied?
cards.back:
primary
secondary
tertiary
quaternary
cards.quote: Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels, i.e., primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary, each level being more complex than the previous one.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the primary structure of a protein?
cards.back: Each polypeptide in a protein has amino acids linked with each other in a specific sequence and it is this sequence of amino acids that is said to be the primary structure of that protein.
cards.quote: Each polypeptide in a protein has amino acids linked with each other in a specific sequence and it is this sequence of amino acids that is said to be the primary structure of that protein.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What happens if the sequence of amino acids in a protein changes?
cards.back: Any change in this primary structure i.e., the sequence of amino acids creates a different protein.
cards.quote: Any change in this primary structure i.e., the sequence of amino acids creates a different protein.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does the secondary structure of a protein refer to?
cards.back: The secondary structure of protein refers to the shape in which a long polypeptide chain can exist.
cards.quote: The secondary structure of protein refers to the shape in which a long polypeptide chain can exist.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does the tertiary structure of proteins represent?
cards.back: The tertiary structure of proteins represents overall folding of the polypeptide chains i.e., further folding of the secondary structure.
cards.quote: The tertiary structure of proteins represents overall folding of the polypeptide chains i.e., further folding of the secondary structure.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The tertiary structure of proteins gives rise to which two major molecular shapes?
cards.back:
fibrous
globular
cards.quote: It gives rise to two major molecular shapes viz. fibrous and globular.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which forces stabilise the 2° and 3° structures of proteins?
cards.back: The main forces which stabilise the 2° and 3° structures of proteins are hydrogen bonds, disulphide linkages, van der Waals and electrostatic forces of attraction.
cards.quote: The main forces which stabilise the 2° and 3° structures of proteins are hydrogen bonds, disulphide linkages, van der Waals and electrostatic forces of attraction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the quaternary structure of a protein?
cards.back: Some of the proteins are composed of two or more polypeptide chains referred to as sub-units. The spatial arrangement of these subunits with respect to each other is known as quaternary structure.
cards.quote: Some of the proteins are composed of two or more polypeptide chains referred to as sub-units. The spatial arrangement of these subunits with respect to each other is known as quaternary structure.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a native protein?
cards.back: Protein found in a biological system with a unique three-dimensional structure and biological activity is called a native protein.
cards.quote: Protein found in a biological system with a unique three-dimensional structure and biological activity is called a native protein.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is denaturation of a protein?
cards.back: When a protein in its native form, is subjected to physical change like change in temperature or chemical change like change in pH, the hydrogen bonds are disturbed. Due to this, globules unfold and helix get uncoiled and protein loses its biological activity. This is called denaturation of protein.
cards.quote: When a protein in its native form, is subjected to physical change like change in temperature or chemical change like change in pH, the hydrogen bonds are disturbed. Due to this, globules unfold and helix get uncoiled and protein loses its biological activity. This is called denaturation of protein.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which structures of a protein are destroyed on denaturation, and which remains intact?
cards.back: During denaturation secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed but primary structure remains intact.
cards.quote: During denaturation secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed but primary structure remains intact.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a common example of denaturation of protein on boiling?
cards.back: coagulation of egg white
cards.quote: The coagulation of egg white on boiling is a common example of denaturation.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What causes the curdling of milk, an example of denaturation?
cards.back: Another example is curdling of milk which is caused due to the formation of lactic acid by the bacteria present in milk.
cards.quote: Another example is curdling of milk which is caused due to the formation of lactic acid by the bacteria present in milk.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How specific are enzymes?
cards.back: Enzymes are very specific for a particular reaction and for a particular substrate.
cards.quote: Enzymes are very specific for a particular reaction and for a particular substrate.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which enzyme catalyses the hydrolysis of maltose into glucose?
cards.back: maltase
cards.quote: For example, the enzyme that catalyses hydrolysis of maltose into glucose is named as maltase.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The enzymes which catalyse the oxidation of one substrate with simultaneous reduction of another substrate are named as ____ enzymes.
cards.back: the enzymes which catalyse the oxidation of one substrate with simultaneous reduction of another substrate are named as oxidoreductase enzymes.
cards.quote: the enzymes which catalyse the oxidation of one substrate with simultaneous reduction of another substrate are named as oxidoreductase enzymes.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The ending of the name of an enzyme is ____.
cards.back: The ending of the name of an enzyme is -ase.
cards.quote: The ending of the name of an enzyme is -ase.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do enzymes, like chemical catalysts, speed up a reaction?
cards.back: Similar to the action of chemical catalysts, enzymes are said to reduce the magnitude of activation energy.
cards.quote: Similar to the action of chemical catalysts, enzymes are said to reduce the magnitude of activation energy.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Activation energy of acid hydrolysis of sucrose versus hydrolysis by the enzyme sucrase
cards.back: activation energy for acid hydrolysis of sucrose is 6.22 kJ mol–1, while the activation energy is only 2.15 kJ mol–1 when hydrolysed by the enzyme, sucrase.
cards.quote: activation energy for acid hydrolysis of sucrose is 6.22 kJ mol–1, while the activation energy is only 2.15 kJ mol–1 when hydrolysed by the enzyme, sucrase.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are vitamins?
cards.back: certain organic compounds are required in small amounts in our diet but their deficiency causes specific diseases. These compounds are called vitamins.
cards.quote: certain organic compounds are required in small amounts in our diet but their deficiency causes specific diseases. These compounds are called vitamins.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why are vitamins considered essential food factors?
cards.back: Most of the vitamins cannot be synthesised in our body but plants can synthesise almost all of them, so they are considered as essential food factors.
cards.quote: Most of the vitamins cannot be synthesised in our body but plants can synthesise almost all of them, so they are considered as essential food factors.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How are vitamins designated?
cards.back: by alphabets A, B, C, D, etc.
cards.quote: Vitamins are designated by alphabets A, B, C, D, etc.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which vitamins are fat soluble?
cards.back: Fat soluble vitamins: Vitamins which are soluble in fat and oils but insoluble in water are kept in this group. These are vitamins A, D, E and K.
cards.quote: Fat soluble vitamins: Vitamins which are soluble in fat and oils but insoluble in water are kept in this group. These are vitamins A, D, E and K.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Where are fat soluble vitamins stored?
cards.back: liver and adipose (fat storing) tissues
cards.quote: They are stored in liver and adipose (fat storing) tissues.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which vitamins are water soluble?
cards.back: Water soluble vitamins: B group vitamins and vitamin C are soluble in water so they are grouped together.
cards.quote: Water soluble vitamins: B group vitamins and vitamin C are soluble in water so they are grouped together.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why must water soluble vitamins be supplied regularly in the diet?
cards.back: Water soluble vitamins must be supplied regularly in diet because they are readily excreted in urine and cannot be stored (except vitamin B12) in our body.
cards.quote: Water soluble vitamins must be supplied regularly in diet because they are readily excreted in urine and cannot be stored (except vitamin B12) in our body.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How are vitamins classified?
cards.back:
fat soluble (A, D, E and K)
water soluble (B group and C)
cards.quote: They are classified as fat soluble (A, D, E and K) and water soluble (B group and C).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Deficiency diseases of vitamin A
cards.back: Xerophthalmia (hardening of cornea of eye) Night blindness
cards.quote: Xerophthalmia (hardening of cornea of eye) Night blindness

cards.quote: Increased fragility of RBCs and muscular weakness

cards.back: Yeast, milk, green vegetables and cereals

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are the particles in the nucleus responsible for heredity called, and what are they made of?
cards.back: The particles in nucleus of the cell, responsible for heredity, are called chromosomes which are made up of proteins and another type of biomolecules called nucleic acids.
cards.quote: The particles in nucleus of the cell, responsible for heredity, are called chromosomes which are made up of proteins and another type of biomolecules called nucleic acids.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Nucleic acids are mainly of which two types?
cards.back:
deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA)
ribonucleic acid (RNA)
cards.quote: These are mainly of two types, the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Since nucleic acids are long chain polymers of nucleotides, so they are also called ____.
cards.back: Since nucleic acids are long chain polymers of nucleotides, so they are also called polynucleotides.
cards.quote: Since nucleic acids are long chain polymers of nucleotides, so they are also called polynucleotides.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does complete hydrolysis of DNA (or RNA) yield?
cards.back: Complete hydrolysis of DNA (or RNA) yields a pentose sugar, phosphoric acid and nitrogen containing heterocyclic compounds (called bases).
cards.quote: Complete hydrolysis of DNA (or RNA) yields a pentose sugar, phosphoric acid and nitrogen containing heterocyclic compounds (called bases).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the four bases in DNA.
cards.back:
adenine (A)
guanine (G)
cytosine (C)
thymine (T)
cards.quote: DNA contains four bases viz. adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which bases does RNA contain, compared with DNA?
cards.back: RNA also contains four bases, the first three bases are same as in DNA but the fourth one is uracil (U).
cards.quote: RNA also contains four bases, the first three bases are same as in DNA but the fourth one is uracil (U).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a nucleoside?
cards.back: A unit formed by the attachment of a base to 1′ position of sugar is known as nucleoside.
cards.quote: A unit formed by the attachment of a base to 1′ position of sugar is known as nucleoside.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a nucleotide?
cards.back: When nucleoside is linked to phosphoric acid at 5′-position of sugar moiety, we get a nucleotide
cards.quote: When nucleoside is linked to phosphoric acid at 5′-position of sugar moiety, we get a nucleotide

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How are nucleotides joined together in a nucleic acid?
cards.back: Nucleotides are joined together by phosphodiester linkage between 5′ and 3′ carbon atoms of the pentose sugar.
cards.quote: Nucleotides are joined together by phosphodiester linkage between 5′ and 3′ carbon atoms of the pentose sugar.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the primary structure of a nucleic acid?
cards.back: Information regarding the sequence of nucleotides in the chain of a nucleic acid is called its primary structure.
cards.quote: Information regarding the sequence of nucleotides in the chain of a nucleic acid is called its primary structure.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Who gave the double strand helix structure for DNA?
cards.back: James Watson and Francis Crick gave a double strand helix structure for DNA
cards.quote: James Watson and Francis Crick gave a double strand helix structure for DNA

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What holds the two chains of the DNA double helix together?
cards.back: Two nucleic acid chains are wound about each other and held together by hydrogen bonds between pairs of bases.
cards.quote: Two nucleic acid chains are wound about each other and held together by hydrogen bonds between pairs of bases.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why are the two strands of DNA complementary? Which bases pair?
cards.back: The two strands are complementary to each other because the hydrogen bonds are formed between specific pairs of bases. Adenine forms hydrogen bonds with thymine whereas cytosine forms hydrogen bonds with guanine.
cards.quote: The two strands are complementary to each other because the hydrogen bonds are formed between specific pairs of bases. Adenine forms hydrogen bonds with thymine whereas cytosine forms hydrogen bonds with guanine.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the three types of RNA molecules.
cards.back:
messenger RNA (m-RNA)
ribosomal RNA (r-RNA)
transfer RNA (t-RNA)
cards.quote: RNA molecules are of three types and they perform different functions. They are named as messenger RNA (m-RNA), ribosomal RNA (r-RNA) and transfer RNA (t-RNA).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is DNA fingerprinting?
cards.back: A sequence of bases on DNA is also unique for a person and information regarding this is called DNA fingerprinting.
cards.quote: A sequence of bases on DNA is also unique for a person and information regarding this is called DNA fingerprinting.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the four uses of DNA fingerprinting.
cards.back:
in forensic laboratories for identification of criminals
to determine paternity of an individual
to identify the dead bodies in any accident by comparing the DNA’s of parents or children
to identify racial groups to rewrite biological evolution
cards.quote: DNA fingerprinting is now used (i) in forensic laboratories for identification of criminals. (ii) to determine paternity of an individual. (iii) to identify the dead bodies in any accident by comparing the DNA’s of parents or children. (iv) to identify racial groups to rewrite biological evolution.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the chemical basis of heredity?
cards.back: DNA
cards.quote: DNA is the chemical basis of heredity and may be regarded as the reserve of genetic information.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is exclusively responsible for maintaining the identity of different species over millions of years?
cards.back: DNA
cards.quote: DNA is exclusively responsible for maintaining the identity of different species of organisms over millions of years.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What happens to a DNA molecule during cell division?
cards.back: A DNA molecule is capable of self duplication during cell division and identical DNA strands are transferred to daughter cells.
cards.quote: A DNA molecule is capable of self duplication during cell division and identical DNA strands are transferred to daughter cells.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What role do nucleic acids play in protein synthesis?
cards.back: Another important function of nucleic acids is the protein synthesis in the cell. Actually, the proteins are synthesised by various RNA molecules in the cell but the message for the synthesis of a particular protein is present in DNA.
cards.quote: Another important function of nucleic acids is the protein synthesis in the cell. Actually, the proteins are synthesised by various RNA molecules in the cell but the message for the synthesis of a particular protein is present in DNA.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Of what do the nucleotides in nucleic acids consist?
cards.back: Nucleic acids are the polymers of nucleotides which in turn consist of a base, a pentose sugar and phosphate moiety.
cards.quote: Nucleic acids are the polymers of nucleotides which in turn consist of a base, a pentose sugar and phosphate moiety.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: DNA vs RNA: the difference on the sugar
cards.back: DNA contains a five carbon sugar molecule called 2-deoxyribose whereas RNA contains ribose.
cards.quote: DNA contains a five carbon sugar molecule called 2-deoxyribose whereas RNA contains ribose.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: DNA vs RNA: the difference on the fourth base
cards.back: Both DNA and RNA contain adenine, guanine and cytosine. The fourth base is thymine in DNA and uracil in RNA.
cards.quote: Both DNA and RNA contain adenine, guanine and cytosine. The fourth base is thymine in DNA and uracil in RNA.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: DNA vs RNA: the difference on the number of strands
cards.back: The structure of DNA is a double strand whereas RNA is a single strand molecule.
cards.quote: The structure of DNA is a double strand whereas RNA is a single strand molecule.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are hormones?
cards.back: Hormones are molecules that act as intercellular messengers. These are produced by endocrine glands in the body and are poured directly in the blood stream which transports them to the site of action.
cards.quote: Hormones are molecules that act as intercellular messengers. These are produced by endocrine glands in the body and are poured directly in the blood stream which transports them to the site of action.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Classify hormones by chemical nature, with examples.
cards.back:
steroids, e.g., estrogens and androgens
poly peptides for example insulin and endorphins
amino acid derivatives such as epinephrine and norepinephrine
cards.quote: In terms of chemical nature, some of these are steroids, e.g., estrogens and androgens; some are poly peptides for example insulin and endorphins and some others are amino acid derivatives such as epinephrine and norepinephrine.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do hormones help in the body, with the example of insulin?
cards.back: They help to maintain the balance of biological activities in the body. The role of insulin in keeping the blood glucose level within the narrow limit is an example of this function.
cards.quote: They help to maintain the balance of biological activities in the body. The role of insulin in keeping the blood glucose level within the narrow limit is an example of this function.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do insulin and glucagon regulate the blood glucose level?
cards.back: Insulin is released in response to the rapid rise in blood glucose level. On the other hand hormone glucagon tends to increase the glucose level in the blood. The two hormones together regulate the glucose level in the blood.
cards.quote: Insulin is released in response to the rapid rise in blood glucose level. On the other hand hormone glucagon tends to increase the glucose level in the blood. The two hormones together regulate the glucose level in the blood.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are the roles of epinephrine, norepinephrine, growth hormones and sex hormones?
cards.back: Epinephrine and norepinephrine mediate responses to external stimuli. Growth hormones and sex hormones play role in growth and development.
cards.quote: Epinephrine and norepinephrine mediate responses to external stimuli. Growth hormones and sex hormones play role in growth and development.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is thyroxine, and where is it produced?
cards.back: Thyroxine produced in the thyroid gland is an iodinated derivative of amino acid tyrosine.
cards.quote: Thyroxine produced in the thyroid gland is an iodinated derivative of amino acid tyrosine.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does an abnormally low level of thyroxine lead to?
cards.back: Abnormally low level of thyroxine leads to hypothyroidism which is characterised by lethargyness and obesity.
cards.quote: Abnormally low level of thyroxine leads to hypothyroidism which is characterised by lethargyness and obesity.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does an increased level of thyroxine cause?
cards.back: hyperthyroidism
cards.quote: Increased level of thyroxine causes hyperthyroidism.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What may a low level of iodine in the diet lead to?
cards.back: Low level of iodine in the diet may lead to hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland.
cards.quote: Low level of iodine in the diet may lead to hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is hypothyroidism due to low iodine largely controlled?
cards.back: This condition is largely being controlled by adding sodium iodide to commercial table salt (“Iodised” salt).
cards.quote: This condition is largely being controlled by adding sodium iodide to commercial table salt (“Iodised” salt).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Where are steroid hormones produced?
cards.back: Steroid hormones are produced by adrenal cortex and gonads (testes in males and ovaries in females).
cards.quote: Steroid hormones are produced by adrenal cortex and gonads (testes in males and ovaries in females).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What do glucocorticoids do?
cards.back: glucocorticoids control the carbohydrate metabolism, modulate inflammatory reactions, and are involved in reactions to stress.
cards.quote: glucocorticoids control the carbohydrate metabolism, modulate inflammatory reactions, and are involved in reactions to stress.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What do mineralocorticoids control?
cards.back: The mineralocorticoids control the level of excretion of water and salt by the kidney.
cards.quote: The mineralocorticoids control the level of excretion of water and salt by the kidney.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What may result if the adrenal cortex does not function properly?
cards.back: If adrenal cortex does not function properly then one of the results may be Addison’s disease characterised by hypoglycemia, weakness and increased susceptibility to stress.
cards.quote: If adrenal cortex does not function properly then one of the results may be Addison’s disease characterised by hypoglycemia, weakness and increased susceptibility to stress.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which is the major male sex hormone, and what does it do?
cards.back: Testosterone is the major sex hormone produced in males. It is responsible for development of secondary male characteristics (deep voice, facial hair, general physical constitution)
cards.quote: Testosterone is the major sex hormone produced in males. It is responsible for development of secondary male characteristics (deep voice, facial hair, general physical constitution)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which is the main female sex hormone, and what does it do?
cards.back: estradiol is the main female sex hormone. It is responsible for development of secondary female characteristics and participates in the control of menstrual cycle.
cards.quote: estradiol is the main female sex hormone. It is responsible for development of secondary female characteristics and participates in the control of menstrual cycle.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is progesterone responsible for?
cards.back: Progesterone is responsible for preparing the uterus for implantation of fertilised egg.
cards.quote: Progesterone is responsible for preparing the uterus for implantation of fertilised egg.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is chemical kinetics?
cards.back: the branch of chemistry, which deals with the study of reaction rates and their mechanisms, called chemical kinetics.
cards.quote: the branch of chemistry, which deals with the study of reaction rates and their mechanisms, called chemical kinetics.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does thermodynamics tell about a reaction, and what does chemical kinetics tell?
cards.back: Thermodynamics tells only about the feasibility of a reaction whereas chemical kinetics tells about the rate of a reaction.
cards.quote: Thermodynamics tells only about the feasibility of a reaction whereas chemical kinetics tells about the rate of a reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the factors that affect the rate of a reaction.
cards.back:
concentration
temperature
pressure
catalyst
cards.quote: The factors such as concentration, temperature, pressure and catalyst affect the rate of a reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define the rate of a reaction.
cards.back: the speed of a reaction or the rate of a reaction can be defined as the change in concentration of a reactant or product in unit time.
cards.quote: the speed of a reaction or the rate of a reaction can be defined as the change in concentration of a reactant or product in unit time.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In which two ways can the rate of a reaction be expressed?
cards.back:
the rate of decrease in concentration of any one of the reactants
the rate of increase in concentration of any one of the products
cards.quote: (i) the rate of decrease in concentration of any one of the reactants, or (ii) the rate of increase in concentration of any one of the products.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is the change in concentration of a reactant multiplied by -1 when the rate is expressed?
cards.back: it is multiplied with -1 to make the rate of the reaction a positive quantity.
cards.quote: it is multiplied with -1 to make the rate of the reaction a positive quantity.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are the units of the rate of a reaction in terms of concentration and time?
cards.back: units of rate are concentration time-1.
cards.quote: From equations (3.1) and (3.2), it is clear that units of rate are concentration time-1.

source.section: Units of rate of a reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are the units of the rate equation in gaseous reactions when concentration is expressed as partial pressure?
cards.back: in gaseous reactions, when the concentration of gases is expressed in terms of their partial pressures, then the units of the rate equation will be atm s-1.
cards.quote: in gaseous reactions, when the concentration of gases is expressed in terms of their partial pressures, then the units of the rate equation will be atm s-1.

source.section: Units of rate of a reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why can the average rate not be used to predict the rate of a reaction at a particular instant?
cards.back: average rate cannot be used to predict the rate of a reaction at a particular instant as it would be constant for the time interval for which it is calculated.
cards.quote: average rate cannot be used to predict the rate of a reaction at a particular instant as it would be constant for the time interval for which it is calculated.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is the instantaneous rate obtained from the average rate?
cards.back: It is obtained when we consider the average rate at the smallest time interval say dt
cards.quote: It is obtained when we consider the average rate at the smallest time interval say dt

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How can the instantaneous rate be determined graphically?
cards.back: It can be determined graphically by drawing a tangent at time t on either of the curves for concentration of R and P vs time t and calculating its slope
cards.quote: It can be determined graphically by drawing a tangent at time t on either of the curves for concentration of R and P vs time t and calculating its slope

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is the rate expressed when stoichiometric coefficients are not equal to one, as in 2HI(g) → H2(g) + I2(g)?
cards.back: For expressing the rate of such a reaction where stoichiometric coefficients of reactants or products are not equal to one, rate of disappearance of any of the reactants or the rate of appearance of products is divided by their respective stoichiometric coefficients.
cards.quote: For expressing the rate of such a reaction where stoichiometric coefficients of reactants or products are not equal to one, rate of disappearance of any of the reactants or the rate of appearance of products is divided by their respective stoichiometric coefficients.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is rate law? Name its other two names.
cards.back: The representation of rate of reaction in terms of concentration of the reactants is known as rate law. It is also called as rate equation or rate expression.
cards.quote: The representation of rate of reaction in terms of concentration of the reactants is known as rate law. It is also called as rate equation or rate expression.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Rate law (3.4a) for aA + bB → cC + dD, with x and y the exponents of [A] and [B].
cards.back: Rate = k [A]x [B]y
cards.quote: Rate = k [A]x [B]y

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In Rate = k [A]x [B]y, what is k called?
cards.back: where k is a proportionality constant called rate constant.
cards.quote: where k is a proportionality constant called rate constant.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define rate constant.
cards.back: Rate constant is the proportionality factor in the rate law.
cards.quote: Rate constant is the proportionality factor in the rate law.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Experimental rate equation for 2NO(g) + O2(g) → 2NO2(g) (Table 3.2).
cards.back: Rate = k [NO]2[O2]
cards.quote: Hence, the rate equation for this reaction will be Rate = k [NO]2[O2]

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Experimental rate expression for CH3COOC2H5 + H2O → CH3COOH + C2H5OH.
cards.back: Rate = k [CH3COOC2H5]1 [H2O]0
cards.quote: Rate = k [CH3COOC2H5]1 [H2O]0

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Rate law for any reaction cannot be predicted by merely looking at the balanced chemical equation, i.e., theoretically but must be determined ____.
cards.back: Rate law for any reaction cannot be predicted by merely looking at the balanced chemical equation, i.e., theoretically but must be determined experimentally.
cards.quote: Rate law for any reaction cannot be predicted by merely looking at the balanced chemical equation, i.e., theoretically but must be determined experimentally.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define the order of a reaction.
cards.back: Hence, the sum of powers of the concentration of the reactants in the rate law expression is called the order of that chemical reaction.
cards.quote: Hence, the sum of powers of the concentration of the reactants in the rate law expression is called the order of that chemical reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In Rate = k [A]x [B]y, what does x + y give, and what do x and y represent?
cards.back: Sum of these exponents, i.e., x + y in (3.4) gives the overall order of a reaction whereas x and y represent the order with respect to the reactants A and B respectively.
cards.quote: Sum of these exponents, i.e., x + y in (3.4) gives the overall order of a reaction whereas x and y represent the order with respect to the reactants A and B respectively.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Order of a reaction can be 0, 1, 2, 3 and even a ____.
cards.back: Order of a reaction can be 0, 1, 2, 3 and even a fraction.
cards.quote: Order of a reaction can be 0, 1, 2, 3 and even a fraction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: A zero order reaction means that the rate of reaction is ____ of the concentration of reactants.
cards.back: A zero order reaction means that the rate of reaction is independent of the concentration of reactants.
cards.quote: A zero order reaction means that the rate of reaction is independent of the concentration of reactants.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are elementary reactions?
cards.back: The reactions taking place in one step are called elementary reactions.
cards.quote: The reactions taking place in one step are called elementary reactions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are complex reactions?
cards.back: When a sequence of elementary reactions (called mechanism) gives us the products, the reactions are called complex reactions.
cards.quote: When a sequence of elementary reactions (called mechanism) gives us the products, the reactions are called complex reactions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Types of complex reactions (as given by NCERT).
cards.back:
consecutive reactions
reverse reactions
side reactions
cards.quote: These may be consecutive reactions (e.g., oxidation of ethane to CO2 and H2O passes through a series of intermediate steps in which alcohol, aldehyde and acid are formed), reverse reactions and side reactions (e.g., nitration of phenol yields o-nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the unit of the rate constant of a first order reaction?
cards.back: The unit of a first order rate constant is s-1
cards.quote: The unit of a first order rate constant is s-1

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the unit of the rate constant of a second order reaction?
cards.back: The unit of second order rate constant is L mol-1 s-1
cards.quote: The unit of second order rate constant is L mol-1 s-1

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Units of the rate constant k for a zero order reaction (Table 3.4).
cards.back: mol L-1s-1
cards.quote: conc time-1 or mol L-1s-1

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define molecularity of a reaction.
cards.back: The number of reacting species (atoms, ions or molecules) taking part in an elementary reaction, which must collide simultaneously in order to bring about a chemical reaction is called molecularity of a reaction.
cards.quote: The number of reacting species (atoms, ions or molecules) taking part in an elementary reaction, which must collide simultaneously in order to bring about a chemical reaction is called molecularity of a reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: When is a reaction unimolecular? Give NCERT's example.
cards.back: The reaction can be unimolecular when one reacting species is involved, for example, decomposition of ammonium nitrite.
cards.quote: The reaction can be unimolecular when one reacting species is involved, for example, decomposition of ammonium nitrite.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What do bimolecular reactions involve? Give NCERT's example.
cards.back: Bimolecular reactions involve simultaneous collision between two species, for example, dissociation of hydrogen iodide.
cards.quote: Bimolecular reactions involve simultaneous collision between two species, for example, dissociation of hydrogen iodide.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What do trimolecular or termolecular reactions involve?
cards.back: Trimolecular or termolecular reactions involve simultaneous collision between three reacting species
cards.quote: Trimolecular or termolecular reactions involve simultaneous collision between three reacting species

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: KClO3 + 6FeSO4 + 3H2SO4 → KCl + 3Fe2(SO4)3 + 3H2O appears to have a very high order. What is its actual order?
cards.back: This reaction which apparently seems to be of tenth order is actually a second order reaction.
cards.quote: This reaction which apparently seems to be of tenth order is actually a second order reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the rate determining step?
cards.back: the overall rate of the reaction is controlled by the slowest step in a reaction called the rate determining step.
cards.quote: the overall rate of the reaction is controlled by the slowest step in a reaction called the rate determining step.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is an intermediate, as IO- in the iodide-catalysed decomposition of H2O2?
cards.back: Species IO- is called as an intermediate since it is formed during the course of the reaction but not in the overall balanced equation.
cards.quote: Species IO- is called as an intermediate since it is formed during the course of the reaction but not in the overall balanced equation.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Order vs molecularity: the difference on nature and possible values.
cards.back: Order of a reaction is an experimental quantity. It can be zero and even a fraction but molecularity cannot be zero or a non integer.
cards.quote: Order of a reaction is an experimental quantity. It can be zero and even a fraction but molecularity cannot be zero or a non integer.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Order vs molecularity: the difference on the type of reaction they apply to.
cards.back: Order is applicable to elementary as well as complex reactions whereas molecularity is applicable only for elementary reactions. For complex reaction molecularity has no meaning.
cards.quote: Order is applicable to elementary as well as complex reactions whereas molecularity is applicable only for elementary reactions. For complex reaction molecularity has no meaning.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: For a complex reaction, how is the order given?
cards.back: For complex reaction, order is given by the slowest step and molecularity of the slowest step is same as the order of the overall reaction.
cards.quote: For complex reaction, order is given by the slowest step and molecularity of the slowest step is same as the order of the overall reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define a zero order reaction.
cards.back: Zero order reaction means that the rate of the reaction is proportional to zero power of the concentration of reactants.
cards.quote: Zero order reaction means that the rate of the reaction is proportional to zero power of the concentration of reactants.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Integrated rate equation (3.6) for a zero order reaction R → P.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Give examples of zero order reactions.
cards.back: Some enzyme catalysed reactions and reactions which occur on metal surfaces are a few examples of zero order reactions.
cards.quote: Some enzyme catalysed reactions and reactions which occur on metal surfaces are a few examples of zero order reactions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which decomposition on a hot platinum surface is a zero order reaction at high pressure?
cards.back: The decomposition of gaseous ammonia on a hot platinum surface is a zero order reaction at high pressure.
cards.quote: The decomposition of gaseous ammonia on a hot platinum surface is a zero order reaction at high pressure.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Integrated rate equation (3.9) for a first order reaction R → P.
cards.back: ln[R] = −kt + ln[R]0
cards.quote: ln[R] = −kt + ln[R]0

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Exponential form (3.14) of the first order integrated rate equation.
cards.back: [R] = [R]0 e−kt
cards.quote: [R] = [R]0 e−kt

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What do we get on plotting ln [R] against t for a first order reaction?
cards.back: if we plot ln [R] against t (Fig. 3.4) we get a straight line with slope = −k and intercept equal to ln [R]0
cards.quote: if we plot ln [R] against t (Fig. 3.4) we get a straight line with slope = −k and intercept equal to ln [R]0

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which hydrogenation reaction is an example of a first order reaction?
cards.back: Hydrogenation of ethene is an example of first order reaction.
cards.quote: Hydrogenation of ethene is an example of first order reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: All natural and artificial radioactive decay of unstable nuclei take place by ____ kinetics.
cards.back: All natural and artificial radioactive decay of unstable nuclei take place by first order kinetics.
cards.quote: All natural and artificial radioactive decay of unstable nuclei take place by first order kinetics.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define the half-life of a reaction.
cards.back: The half-life of a reaction is the time in which the concentration of a reactant is reduced to one half of its initial concentration. It is represented as t1/2.
cards.quote: The half-life of a reaction is the time in which the concentration of a reactant is reduced to one half of its initial concentration. It is represented as t1/2.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How does t1/2 of a zero order reaction depend on the initial concentration and the rate constant?
cards.back: It is clear that t1/2 for a zero order reaction is directly proportional to the initial concentration of the reactants and inversely proportional to the rate constant.
cards.quote: It is clear that t1/2 for a zero order reaction is directly proportional to the initial concentration of the reactants and inversely proportional to the rate constant.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Formula: half-life of a first order reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In a first order reaction, how does the time required for 99.9% completion compare with the half-life?
cards.back: time required for completion of 99.9% is 10 times of half-life (t1/2) of the reaction.
cards.quote: time required for completion of 99.9% is 10 times of half-life (t1/2) of the reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Hydrolysis of ethyl acetate is really second order. Why does it follow a first order rate law?
cards.back: But water is taken in large excess for hydrolysis, therefore, concentration of water is not altered much during the reaction.
cards.quote: But water is taken in large excess for hydrolysis, therefore, concentration of water is not altered much during the reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which reaction of cane sugar is another pseudo first order reaction?
cards.back: Inversion of cane sugar is another pseudo first order reaction.
cards.quote: Inversion of cane sugar is another pseudo first order reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Rate law for the inversion of cane sugar (pseudo first order).
cards.back: Rate = k [C12H22O11]
cards.quote: Rate = k [C12H22O11]

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: By what factor does the rate constant change for a rise in temperature of 10°?
cards.back: It has been found that for a chemical reaction with rise in temperature by 10°, the rate constant is nearly doubled.
cards.quote: It has been found that for a chemical reaction with rise in temperature by 10°, the rate constant is nearly doubled.

source.section: 3.4 Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Formula: Arrhenius equation.
cards.back: k = Ae−Ea/RT
cards.quote: Temperature dependence of rate constants is described by Arrhenius equation (k = Ae−Ea/RT).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is A in the Arrhenius equation? Name its other names.
cards.back: where A is the Arrhenius factor or the frequency factor. It is also called pre-exponential factor. It is a constant specific to a particular reaction.
cards.quote: where A is the Arrhenius factor or the frequency factor. It is also called pre-exponential factor. It is a constant specific to a particular reaction.

source.section: 3.4 Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define activation energy (Ea).
cards.back: The energy required to form this intermediate, called activated complex (C), is known as activation energy (Ea).
cards.quote: The energy required to form this intermediate, called activated complex (C), is known as activation energy (Ea).

source.section: 3.4 Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The peak of the curve corresponds to the ____, i.e., kinetic energy of maximum fraction of molecules.
cards.back: The peak of the curve corresponds to the most probable kinetic energy, i.e., kinetic energy of maximum fraction of molecules.
cards.quote: The peak of the curve corresponds to the most probable kinetic energy, i.e., kinetic energy of maximum fraction of molecules.

source.section: 3.4 Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What happens to the kinetic energy distribution curve when the temperature is raised?
cards.back: the maximum of the curve moves to the higher energy value (Fig. 3.9) and the curve broadens out, i.e., spreads to the right such that there is a greater proportion of molecules with much higher energies.
cards.quote: the maximum of the curve moves to the higher energy value (Fig. 3.9) and the curve broadens out, i.e., spreads to the right such that there is a greater proportion of molecules with much higher energies.

source.section: 3.4 Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In the Arrhenius equation, what does the factor e-Ea/RT correspond to?
cards.back: corresponds to the fraction of molecules that have kinetic energy greater than Ea.
cards.quote: corresponds to the fraction of molecules that have kinetic energy greater than Ea.

source.section: 3.4 Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: According to the Arrhenius equation, what increases the rate of reaction and the rate constant?
cards.back: Thus, it has been found from Arrhenius equation (3.18) that increasing the temperature or decreasing the activation energy will result in an increase in the rate of the reaction and an exponential increase in the rate constant.
cards.quote: Thus, it has been found from Arrhenius equation (3.18) that increasing the temperature or decreasing the activation energy will result in an increase in the rate of the reaction and an exponential increase in the rate constant.

source.section: 3.4 Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define a catalyst.
cards.back: A catalyst is a substance which increases the rate of a reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change.
cards.quote: A catalyst is a substance which increases the rate of a reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The word catalyst should not be used when the added substance reduces the rate of raction. The substance is then called ____.
cards.back:
inhibitor
The word catalyst should not be used when the added substance reduces the rate of raction. The substance is then called inhibitor.
cards.quote: The word catalyst should not be used when the added substance reduces the rate of raction. The substance is then called inhibitor.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: According to the intermediate complex theory, how does a catalyst participate in a reaction?
cards.back: According to this theory, a catalyst participates in a chemical reaction by forming temporary bonds with the reactants resulting in an intermediate complex.
cards.quote: According to this theory, a catalyst participates in a chemical reaction by forming temporary bonds with the reactants resulting in an intermediate complex.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
cards.back: It is believed that the catalyst provides an alternate pathway or reaction mechanism by reducing the activation energy between reactants and products and hence lowering the potential energy barrier
cards.quote: It is believed that the catalyst provides an alternate pathway or reaction mechanism by reducing the activation energy between reactants and products and hence lowering the potential energy barrier

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which reactions does a catalyst catalyse, and which not?
cards.back: It catalyses the spontaneous reactions but does not catalyse non-spontaneous reactions.
cards.quote: It catalyses the spontaneous reactions but does not catalyse non-spontaneous reactions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Does a catalyst change the equilibrium constant of a reaction?
cards.back: It is also found that a catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant of a reaction rather, it helps in attaining the equilibrium faster, that is, it catalyses the forward as well as the backward reactions to the same extent so that the equilibrium state remains same but is reached earlier.
cards.quote: It is also found that a catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant of a reaction rather, it helps in attaining the equilibrium faster, that is, it catalyses the forward as well as the backward reactions to the same extent so that the equilibrium state remains same but is reached earlier.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In collision theory, what are reactant molecules assumed to be, and when is a reaction postulated to occur?
cards.back: assumed to be hard spheres and reaction is postulated to occur when molecules collide with each other.
cards.quote: assumed to be hard spheres and reaction is postulated to occur when molecules collide with each other.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define collision frequency (Z).
cards.back: The number of collisions per second per unit volume of the reaction mixture is known as collision frequency (Z).
cards.quote: The number of collisions per second per unit volume of the reaction mixture is known as collision frequency (Z).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are effective collisions?
cards.back: The collisions in which molecules collide with sufficient kinetic energy (called threshold energy*) and proper orientation, so as to facilitate breaking of bonds between reacting species and formation of new bonds to form products are called as effective collisions.
cards.quote: The collisions in which molecules collide with sufficient kinetic energy (called threshold energy*) and proper orientation, so as to facilitate breaking of bonds between reacting species and formation of new bonds to form products are called as effective collisions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Formula: threshold energy.
cards.back: Threshold energy = Activation Energy + energy possessed by reacting species.
cards.quote: Threshold energy = Activation Energy + energy possessed by reacting species.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In collision theory, what is the factor P introduced to account for effective collisions called?
cards.back: another factor P, called the probability or steric factor is introduced.
cards.quote: another factor P, called the probability or steric factor is introduced.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In collision theory, what together determine the criteria for an effective collision?
cards.back: Thus, in collision theory activation energy and proper orientation of the molecules together determine the criteria for an effective collision and hence the rate of a chemical reaction.
cards.quote: Thus, in collision theory activation energy and proper orientation of the molecules together determine the criteria for an effective collision and hence the rate of a chemical reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: For which reactions does collision theory predict rate constants fairly accurately, and when do deviations occur?
cards.back: Equation (3.23) predicts the value of rate constants fairly accurately for the reactions that involve atomic species or simple molecules but for complex molecules significant deviations are observed.
cards.quote: Equation (3.23) predicts the value of rate constants fairly accurately for the reactions that involve atomic species or simple molecules but for complex molecules significant deviations are observed.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a drawback of collision theory?
cards.back: Collision theory also has certain drawbacks as it considers atoms/molecules to be hard spheres and ignores their structural aspect.
cards.quote: Collision theory also has certain drawbacks as it considers atoms/molecules to be hard spheres and ignores their structural aspect.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does A in the Arrhenius equation correspond to?
cards.back: A (Arrhenius factor or pre-exponential factor) corresponds to the collision frequency.
cards.quote: A (Arrhenius factor or pre-exponential factor) corresponds to the collision frequency.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are coordination compounds? (NCERT, modern terminology)
cards.back: In the previous Unit we learnt that the transition metals form a large number of complex compounds in which the metal atoms are bound to a number of anions or neutral molecules by sharing of electrons. In modern terminology such compounds are called coordination compounds.
cards.quote: In the previous Unit we learnt that the transition metals form a large number of complex compounds in which the metal atoms are bound to a number of anions or neutral molecules by sharing of electrons. In modern terminology such compounds are called coordination compounds.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Chlorophyll, haemoglobin and vitamin B12 are coordination compounds of which metals respectively?
cards.back: Chlorophyll, haemoglobin and vitamin B12 are coordination compounds of magnesium, iron and cobalt respectively.
cards.quote: Chlorophyll, haemoglobin and vitamin B12 are coordination compounds of magnesium, iron and cobalt respectively.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Who was the first to formulate ideas about the structures of coordination compounds?
cards.back: Alfred Werner (1866-1919), a Swiss chemist was the first to formulate his ideas about the structures of coordination compounds.
cards.quote: Alfred Werner (1866-1919), a Swiss chemist was the first to formulate his ideas about the structures of coordination compounds.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Werner proposed the concept of a primary valence and a ____ for a metal ion.
cards.back: Werner proposed the concept of a primary valence and a secondary valence for a metal ion.
cards.quote: Werner proposed the concept of a primary valence and a secondary valence for a metal ion.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What did Werner mean by the term secondary valence?
cards.back: Werner proposed the term secondary valence for the number of groups bound directly to the metal ion; in each of these examples the secondary valences are six.
cards.quote: Werner proposed the term secondary valence for the number of groups bound directly to the metal ion; in each of these examples the secondary valences are six.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Moles of AgCl given with excess silver nitrate by CoCl3.6NH3 (yellow), CoCl3.5NH3 (purple), CoCl3.4NH3 (green) and CoCl3.4NH3 (violet)?
cards.back:
1 mol CoCl3.6NH3 (Yellow) gave 3 mol AgCl
1 mol CoCl3.5NH3 (Purple) gave 2 mol AgCl
1 mol CoCl3.4NH3 (Green) gave 1 mol AgCl
1 mol CoCl3.4NH3 (Violet) gave 1 mol AgCl
cards.quote: 1 mol CoCl3.6NH3 (Yellow) gave 3 mol AgCl 1 mol CoCl3.5NH3 (Purple) gave 2 mol AgCl 1 mol CoCl3.4NH3 (Green) gave 1 mol AgCl 1 mol CoCl3.4NH3 (Violet) gave 1 mol AgCl

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: State the main postulates of Werner’s theory of coordination compounds.
cards.back:
In coordination compounds metals show two types of linkages (valences)-primary and secondary.
The primary valences are normally ionisable and are satisfied by negative ions.
The secondary valences are non ionisable. These are satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions. The secondary valence is equal to the coordination number and is fixed for a metal.
The ions/groups bound by the secondary linkages to the metal have characteristic spatial arrangements corresponding to different coordination numbers.
cards.quote: 1. In coordination compounds metals show two types of linkages (valences)-primary and secondary. 2. The primary valences are normally ionisable and are satisfied by negative ions. 3. The secondary valences are non ionisable. These are satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions. The secondary valence is equal to the coordination number and is fixed for a metal. 4. The ions/groups bound by the secondary linkages to the metal have characteristic spatial arrangements corresponding to different coordination numbers.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The primary valences are normally ____ and are satisfied by ____.
cards.back: The primary valences are normally ionisable and are satisfied by negative ions.
cards.quote: The primary valences are normally ionisable and are satisfied by negative ions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are coordination entities (complexes) and counter ions in a coordination compound?
cards.back: The species within the square bracket are coordination entities or complexes and the ions outside the square bracket are called counter ions.
cards.quote: The species within the square bracket are coordination entities or complexes and the ions outside the square bracket are called counter ions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which geometrical shapes did Werner postulate to be more common in coordination compounds of transition metals?
cards.back:
octahedral
tetrahedral
square planar
cards.quote: He further postulated that octahedral, tetrahedral and square planar geometrical shapes are more common in coordination compounds of transition metals.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Double salt vs complex: the difference on dissolving in water.
cards.back: However, they differ in the fact that double salts such as carnallite, KCl.MgCl2.6H2O, Mohr’s salt, FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O, potash alum, KAl(SO4)2.12H2O, etc. dissociate into simple ions completely when dissolved in water. However, complex ions such as [Fe(CN)6]4– of K4 [Fe(CN)6] do not dissociate into Fe2+ and CN– ions.
cards.quote: Both double salts as well as complexes are formed by the combination of two or more stable compounds in stoichiometric ratio. However, they differ in the fact that double salts such as carnallite, KCl.MgCl2.6H2O, Mohr’s salt, FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O, potash alum, KAl(SO4)2.12H2O, etc. dissociate into simple ions completely when dissolved in water. However, complex ions such as [Fe(CN)6]4– of K4 [Fe(CN)6] do not dissociate into Fe2+ and CN– ions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Both double salts as well as complexes are formed by the combination of two or more stable compounds in ____.
cards.back: Both double salts as well as complexes are formed by the combination of two or more stable compounds in stoichiometric ratio.
cards.quote: Both double salts as well as complexes are formed by the combination of two or more stable compounds in stoichiometric ratio.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define a coordination entity.
cards.back: A coordination entity constitutes a central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ions or molecules.
cards.quote: A coordination entity constitutes a central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ions or molecules.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the central atom or ion in a coordination entity?
cards.back: In a coordination entity, the atom/ion to which a fixed number of ions/groups are bound in a definite geometrical arrangement around it, is called the central atom or ion.
cards.quote: In a coordination entity, the atom/ion to which a fixed number of ions/groups are bound in a definite geometrical arrangement around it, is called the central atom or ion.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the central atom/ion in [NiCl2(H2O)4], [CoCl(NH3)5]2+ and [Fe(CN)6]3–.
cards.back: For example, the central atom/ion in the coordination entities: [NiCl2(H2O)4], [CoCl(NH3)5]2+ and [Fe(CN)6]3– are Ni2+, Co3+ and Fe3+, respectively.
cards.quote: For example, the central atom/ion in the coordination entities: [NiCl2(H2O)4], [CoCl(NH3)5]2+ and [Fe(CN)6]3– are Ni2+, Co3+ and Fe3+, respectively.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are ligands?
cards.back: The ions or molecules bound to the central atom/ion in the coordination entity are called ligands.
cards.quote: The ions or molecules bound to the central atom/ion in the coordination entity are called ligands.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What kinds of species can act as ligands (NCERT examples)?
cards.back:
simple ions such as Cl–
small molecules such as H2O or NH3
larger molecules such as H2NCH2CH2NH2 or N(CH2CH2NH2)3
macromolecules, such as proteins
cards.quote: These may be simple ions such as Cl–, small molecules such as H2O or NH3, larger molecules such as H2NCH2CH2NH2 or N(CH2CH2NH2)3 or even macromolecules, such as proteins.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a unidentate ligand?
cards.back: When a ligand is bound to a metal ion through a single donor atom, as with Cl–, H2O or NH3, the ligand is said to be unidentate.
cards.quote: When a ligand is bound to a metal ion through a single donor atom, as with Cl–, H2O or NH3, the ligand is said to be unidentate.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a didentate ligand?
cards.back: When a ligand can bind through two donor atoms as in H2NCH2CH2NH2 (ethane-1,2-diamine) or C2O42– (oxalate), the ligand is said to be didentate
cards.quote: When a ligand can bind through two donor atoms as in H2NCH2CH2NH2 (ethane-1,2-diamine) or C2O42– (oxalate), the ligand is said to be didentate

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a polydentate ligand?
cards.back: when several donor atoms are present in a single ligand as in N(CH2CH2NH2)3, the ligand is said to be polydentate.
cards.quote: when several donor atoms are present in a single ligand as in N(CH2CH2NH2)3, the ligand is said to be polydentate.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: EDTA4– is an important ligand of which type, and through which donor atoms does it bind?
cards.back: Ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion (EDTA4–) is an important hexadentate ligand. It can bind through two nitrogen and four oxygen atoms to a central metal ion.
cards.quote: Ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion (EDTA4–) is an important hexadentate ligand. It can bind through two nitrogen and four oxygen atoms to a central metal ion.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a chelate ligand?
cards.back: When a di- or polydentate ligand uses its two or more donor atoms simultaneously to bind a single metal ion, it is said to be a chelate ligand.
cards.quote: When a di- or polydentate ligand uses its two or more donor atoms simultaneously to bind a single metal ion, it is said to be a chelate ligand.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the denticity of a ligand?
cards.back: The number of such ligating groups is called the denticity of the ligand.
cards.quote: The number of such ligating groups is called the denticity of the ligand.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is an ambidentate ligand?
cards.back: Ligand which has two different donor atoms and either of the two ligetes in the complex is called ambidentate ligand.
cards.quote: Ligand which has two different donor atoms and either of the two ligetes in the complex is called ambidentate ligand.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.note: One ligand with two possible donor atoms, binding through either one, e.g. NO2– (N or O).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name two ambidentate ligands (NCERT) and how NO2– can coordinate.
cards.back: Examples of such ligands are the NO2– and SCN– ions. NO2– ion can coordinate either through nitrogen or through oxygen to a central metal atom/ion.
cards.quote: Examples of such ligands are the NO2– and SCN– ions. NO2– ion can coordinate either through nitrogen or through oxygen to a central metal atom/ion.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define the coordination number (CN) of a metal ion in a complex.
cards.back: The coordination number (CN) of a metal ion in a complex can be defined as the number of ligand donor atoms to which the metal is directly bonded.
cards.quote: The coordination number (CN) of a metal ion in a complex can be defined as the number of ligand donor atoms to which the metal is directly bonded.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Coordination number of Pt in [PtCl6]2– and of Ni in [Ni(NH3)4]2+?
cards.back: For example, in the complex ions, [PtCl6]2– and [Ni(NH3)4]2+, the coordination number of Pt and Ni are 6 and 4 respectively.
cards.quote: For example, in the complex ions, [PtCl6]2– and [Ni(NH3)4]2+, the coordination number of Pt and Ni are 6 and 4 respectively.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Coordination number of Fe in [Fe(C2O4)3]3– and Co in [Co(en)3]3+, and why?
cards.back: Similarly, in the complex ions, [Fe(C2O4)3]3– and [Co(en)3]3+, the coordination number of both, Fe and Co, is 6 because C2O42– and en (ethane-1,2-diamine) are didentate ligands.
cards.quote: Similarly, in the complex ions, [Fe(C2O4)3]3– and [Co(en)3]3+, the coordination number of both, Fe and Co, is 6 because C2O42– and en (ethane-1,2-diamine) are didentate ligands.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the coordination sphere?
cards.back: The central atom/ion and the ligands attached to it are enclosed in square bracket and is collectively termed as the coordination sphere.
cards.quote: The central atom/ion and the ligands attached to it are enclosed in square bracket and is collectively termed as the coordination sphere.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The ionisable groups are written outside the bracket and are called ____.
cards.back: The ionisable groups are written outside the bracket and are called counter ions.
cards.quote: The ionisable groups are written outside the bracket and are called counter ions.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In K4[Fe(CN)6], name the coordination sphere and the counter ion.
cards.back: For example, in the complex K4[Fe(CN)6], the coordination sphere is [Fe(CN)6]4– and the counter ion is K+.
cards.quote: For example, in the complex K4[Fe(CN)6], the coordination sphere is [Fe(CN)6]4– and the counter ion is K+.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a coordination polyhedron?
