cards.back: The spatial arrangement of the ligand atoms which are directly attached to the central atom/ion defines a coordination polyhedron about the central atom.
cards.quote: The spatial arrangement of the ligand atoms which are directly attached to the central atom/ion defines a coordination polyhedron about the central atom.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the most common coordination polyhedra.
cards.back:
octahedral
square planar
tetrahedral
cards.quote: The most common coordination polyhedra are octahedral, square planar and tetrahedral.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Shape of [Co(NH3)6]3+, [Ni(CO)4] and [PtCl4]2– (coordination polyhedron)?
cards.back: For example, [Co(NH3)6]3+ is octahedral, [Ni(CO)4] is tetrahedral and [PtCl4]2– is square planar.
cards.quote: For example, [Co(NH3)6]3+ is octahedral, [Ni(CO)4] is tetrahedral and [PtCl4]2– is square planar.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define the oxidation number of the central atom in a complex.
cards.back: The oxidation number of the central atom in a complex is defined as the charge it would carry if all the ligands are removed along with the electron pairs that are shared with the central atom.
cards.quote: The oxidation number of the central atom in a complex is defined as the charge it would carry if all the ligands are removed along with the electron pairs that are shared with the central atom.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The oxidation number is represented by a ____ in parenthesis following the name of the coordination entity.
cards.back: The oxidation number is represented by a Roman numeral in parenthesis following the name of the coordination entity.
cards.quote: The oxidation number is represented by a Roman numeral in parenthesis following the name of the coordination entity.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Oxidation number of copper in [Cu(CN)4]3– and how it is written?
cards.back: For example, oxidation number of copper in [Cu(CN)4]3– is +1 and it is written as Cu(I).
cards.quote: For example, oxidation number of copper in [Cu(CN)4]3– is +1 and it is written as Cu(I).

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Homoleptic vs heteroleptic complexes: the difference on the kinds of donor groups bound to the metal.
cards.back: Complexes in which a metal is bound to only one kind of donor groups, e.g., [Co(NH3)6]3+, are known as homoleptic. Complexes in which a metal is bound to more than one kind of donor groups, e.g., [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+, are known as heteroleptic.
cards.quote: Complexes in which a metal is bound to only one kind of donor groups, e.g., [Co(NH3)6]3+, are known as homoleptic. Complexes in which a metal is bound to more than one kind of donor groups, e.g., [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+, are known as heteroleptic.

source.section: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Order of writing a mononuclear coordination entity formula: central atom and ligands.
cards.back:
The central atom is listed first.
The ligands are then listed in alphabetical order. The placement of a ligand in the list does not depend on its charge.
cards.quote: (i) The central atom is listed first. (ii) The ligands are then listed in alphabetical order. The placement of a ligand in the list does not depend on its charge.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: (v) There should be ____ between the ligands and the metal within a coordination sphere.
cards.back: (v) There should be no space between the ligands and the metal within a coordination sphere.
cards.quote: (v) There should be no space between the ligands and the metal within a coordination sphere.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does the 2004 IUPAC draft recommend about sorting ligands in a formula?
cards.back: The 2004 IUPAC draft recommends that ligands will be sorted alphabetically, irrespective of charge.
cards.quote: The 2004 IUPAC draft recommends that ligands will be sorted alphabetically, irrespective of charge.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The 2004 IUPAC draft recommends that anionic ligands will end with –ido so that chloro would become ____, etc.
cards.back: The 2004 IUPAC draft recommends that anionic ligands will end with –ido so that chloro would become chlorido, etc.
cards.quote: The 2004 IUPAC draft recommends that anionic ligands will end with –ido so that chloro would become chlorido, etc.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The names of coordination compounds are derived by following the principles of ____.
cards.back: The names of coordination compounds are derived by following the principles of additive nomenclature.
cards.quote: The names of coordination compounds are derived by following the principles of additive nomenclature.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: (i) The ____ is named first in both positively and negatively charged coordination entities.
cards.back: (i) The cation is named first in both positively and negatively charged coordination entities.
cards.quote: (i) The cation is named first in both positively and negatively charged coordination entities.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: (ii) The ligands are named in an ____ before the name of the central atom/ion. (This procedure is reversed from writing formula).
cards.back: (ii) The ligands are named in an alphabetical order before the name of the central atom/ion. (This procedure is reversed from writing formula).
cards.quote: (ii) The ligands are named in an alphabetical order before the name of the central atom/ion. (This procedure is reversed from writing formula).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Names of neutral ligands H2O, NH3, CO and NO that differ from their usual names.
cards.back:
aqua for H2O
ammine for NH3
carbonyl for CO
nitrosyl for NO
cards.quote: aqua for H2O, ammine for NH3, carbonyl for CO and nitrosyl for NO.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which terms are used when the names of the ligands themselves include a numerical prefix?
cards.back: When the names of the ligands include a numerical prefix, then the terms, bis, tris, tetrakis are used, the ligand to which they refer being placed in parentheses.
cards.quote: When the names of the ligands include a numerical prefix, then the terms, bis, tris, tetrakis are used, the ligand to which they refer being placed in parentheses.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: IUPAC name of [NiCl2(PPh3)2].
cards.back: dichloridobis(triphenylphosphine)nickel(II)
cards.quote: For example, [NiCl2(PPh3)2] is named as dichloridobis(triphenylphosphine)nickel(II).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: (v) Oxidation state of the metal in cation, anion or neutral coordination entity is indicated by ____ in parenthesis.
cards.back: (v) Oxidation state of the metal in cation, anion or neutral coordination entity is indicated by Roman numeral in parenthesis.
cards.quote: (v) Oxidation state of the metal in cation, anion or neutral coordination entity is indicated by Roman numeral in parenthesis.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is the metal named when the complex ion is a cation?
cards.back: If the complex ion is a cation, the metal is named same as the element. For example, Co in a complex cation is called cobalt and Pt is called platinum.
cards.quote: If the complex ion is a cation, the metal is named same as the element. For example, Co in a complex cation is called cobalt and Pt is called platinum.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is the metal named when the complex ion is an anion?
cards.back: If the complex ion is an anion, the name of the metal ends with the suffix – ate.
cards.quote: If the complex ion is an anion, the name of the metal ends with the suffix – ate.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: For some metals, the Latin names are used in the complex anions, e.g., ____ for Fe.
cards.back: For some metals, the Latin names are used in the complex anions, e.g., ferrate for Fe.
cards.quote: For some metals, the Latin names are used in the complex anions, e.g., ferrate for Fe.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: (vii) The neutral complex molecule is named similar to that of the ____.
cards.back: (vii) The neutral complex molecule is named similar to that of the complex cation.
cards.quote: (vii) The neutral complex molecule is named similar to that of the complex cation.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: IUPAC name of [Cr(NH3)3(H2O)3]Cl3.
cards.back: triamminetriaquachromium(III) chloride
cards.quote: [Cr(NH3)3(H2O)3]Cl3 is named as: triamminetriaquachromium(III) chloride

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: IUPAC name of [Co(H2NCH2CH2NH2)3]2(SO4)3.
cards.back: tris(ethane-1,2–diamine)cobalt(III) sulphate
cards.quote: [Co(H2NCH2CH2NH2)3]2(SO4)3 is named as: tris(ethane-1,2–diamine)cobalt(III) sulphate

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: IUPAC name of [Ag(NH3)2][Ag(CN)2].
cards.back: diamminesilver(I)dicyanidoargentate(I)
cards.quote: [Ag(NH3)2][Ag(CN)2] is named as: diamminesilver(I)dicyanidoargentate(I)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are isomers?
cards.back: Isomers are two or more compounds that have the same chemical formula but a different arrangement of atoms.
cards.quote: Isomers are two or more compounds that have the same chemical formula but a different arrangement of atoms.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Because of the different arrangement of atoms, they differ in one or more ____.
cards.back: Because of the different arrangement of atoms, they differ in one or more physical or chemical properties.
cards.quote: Because of the different arrangement of atoms, they differ in one or more physical or chemical properties.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Types of isomerism in coordination compounds.
cards.back:
(a) Stereoisomerism
(i) Geometrical isomerism
(ii) Optical isomerism
(b) Structural isomerism
(i) Linkage isomerism
(ii) Coordination isomerism
(iii) Ionisation isomerism
(iv) Solvate isomerism
cards.quote: (a) Stereoisomerism (i) Geometrical isomerism (ii) Optical isomerism (b) Structural isomerism (i) Linkage isomerism (ii) Coordination isomerism (iii) Ionisation isomerism (iv) Solvate isomerism

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Types of stereoisomerism in coordination compounds.
cards.back:
(i) Geometrical isomerism
(ii) Optical isomerism
cards.quote: (a) Stereoisomerism (i) Geometrical isomerism (ii) Optical isomerism

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Types of structural isomerism in coordination compounds.
cards.back:
(i) Linkage isomerism
(ii) Coordination isomerism
(iii) Ionisation isomerism
(iv) Solvate isomerism
cards.quote: (b) Structural isomerism (i) Linkage isomerism (ii) Coordination isomerism (iii) Ionisation isomerism (iv) Solvate isomerism

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Stereoisomers vs structural isomers: the difference in bonds and arrangement.
cards.back: Stereoisomers have the same chemical formula and chemical bonds but they have different spatial arrangement. Structural isomers have different bonds.
cards.quote: Stereoisomers have the same chemical formula and chemical bonds but they have different spatial arrangement. Structural isomers have different bonds.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In a square planar complex [MX2L2] (X and L unidentate), what are the cis and trans isomers?
cards.back: the two ligands X may be arranged adjacent to each other in a cis isomer, or opposite to each other in a trans isomer
cards.quote: the two ligands X may be arranged adjacent to each other in a cis isomer, or opposite to each other in a trans isomer

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: A square planar complex of the type MABXL (A, B, X, L unidentates) shows how many isomers?
cards.back: three isomers-two cis and one trans
cards.quote: shows three isomers-two cis and one trans.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is geometrical isomerism not possible in tetrahedral complexes with two different types of unidentate ligands?
cards.back: Tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism because the relative positions of the unidentate ligands attached to the central metal atom are the same with respect to each other.
cards.quote: Tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism because the relative positions of the unidentate ligands attached to the central metal atom are the same with respect to each other.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the facial (fac) isomer of an octahedral [Ma3b3] entity?
cards.back: If three donor atoms of the same ligands occupy adjacent positions at the corners of an octahedral face, we have the facial (fac) isomer.
cards.quote: If three donor atoms of the same ligands occupy adjacent positions at the corners of an octahedral face, we have the facial (fac) isomer.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the meridional (mer) isomer of an octahedral [Ma3b3] entity?
cards.back: When the positions are around the meridian of the octahedron, we get the meridional (mer) isomer
cards.quote: When the positions are around the meridian of the octahedron, we get the meridional (mer) isomer

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are optical isomers?
cards.back: Optical isomers are mirror images that cannot be superimposed on one another. These are called as enantiomers.
cards.quote: Optical isomers are mirror images that cannot be superimposed on one another. These are called as enantiomers.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are chiral molecules or ions?
cards.back: The molecules or ions that cannot be superimposed are called chiral.
cards.quote: The molecules or ions that cannot be superimposed are called chiral.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are the d and l forms of optical isomers?
cards.back: The two forms are called dextro (d) and laevo (l) depending upon the direction they rotate the plane of polarised light in a polarimeter (d rotates to the right, l to the left).
cards.quote: The two forms are called dextro (d) and laevo (l) depending upon the direction they rotate the plane of polarised light in a polarimeter (d rotates to the right, l to the left).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Optical isomerism is common in octahedral complexes involving ____ (Fig. 5.6).
cards.back: Optical isomerism is common in octahedral complexes involving didentate ligands (Fig. 5.6).
cards.quote: Optical isomerism is common in octahedral complexes involving didentate ligands (Fig. 5.6).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In [PtCl2(en)2]2+, which isomer shows optical activity?
cards.back: In a coordination entity of the type [PtCl2(en)2]2+, only the cis-isomer shows optical activity (Fig. 5.7).
cards.quote: In a coordination entity of the type [PtCl2(en)2]2+, only the cis-isomer shows optical activity (Fig. 5.7).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which is chiral (optically active): cis-[CrCl2(ox)2]3– or trans-[CrCl2(ox)2]3–?
cards.back: Out of the two, (a) cis - [CrCl2(ox)2]3- is chiral (optically active).
cards.quote: Out of the two, (a) cis - [CrCl2(ox)2]3- is chiral (optically active).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Linkage isomerism arises in a coordination compound containing ____.
cards.back: Linkage isomerism arises in a coordination compound containing ambidentate ligand.
cards.quote: Linkage isomerism arises in a coordination compound containing ambidentate ligand.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Linkage isomerism with the thiocyanate ligand NCS–: which two linkages are possible?
cards.back: A simple example is provided by complexes containing the thiocyanate ligand, NCS–, which may bind through the nitrogen to give M–NCS or through sulphur to give M–SCN.
cards.quote: A simple example is provided by complexes containing the thiocyanate ligand, NCS–, which may bind through the nitrogen to give M–NCS or through sulphur to give M–SCN.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: [Co(NH3)5(NO2)]Cl2: which colour form has nitrite bound through oxygen and which through nitrogen?
cards.back: Jørgensen discovered such behaviour in the complex [Co(NH3)5(NO2)]Cl2, which is obtained as the red form, in which the nitrite ligand is bound through oxygen (–ONO), and as the yellow form, in which the nitrite ligand is bound through nitrogen (–NO2).
cards.quote: Jørgensen discovered such behaviour in the complex [Co(NH3)5(NO2)]Cl2, which is obtained as the red form, in which the nitrite ligand is bound through oxygen (–ONO), and as the yellow form, in which the nitrite ligand is bound through nitrogen (–NO2).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is coordination isomerism?
cards.back: This type of isomerism arises from the interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic entities of different metal ions present in a complex.
cards.quote: This type of isomerism arises from the interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic entities of different metal ions present in a complex.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Give the coordination isomer of [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6].
cards.back: An example is provided by [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6], in which the NH3 ligands are bound to Co3+ and the CN– ligands to Cr3+. In its coordination isomer [Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6], the NH3 ligands are bound to Cr3+ and the CN– ligands to Co3+.
cards.quote: An example is provided by [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6], in which the NH3 ligands are bound to Co3+ and the CN– ligands to Cr3+. In its coordination isomer [Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6], the NH3 ligands are bound to Cr3+ and the CN– ligands to Co3+.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is ionisation isomerism?
cards.back: This form of isomerism arises when the counter ion in a complex salt is itself a potential ligand and can displace a ligand which can then become the counter ion.
cards.quote: This form of isomerism arises when the counter ion in a complex salt is itself a potential ligand and can displace a ligand which can then become the counter ion.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do solvate isomers differ?
cards.back: Solvate isomers differ by whether or not a solvent molecule is directly bonded to the metal ion or merely present as free solvent molecules in the crystal lattice.
cards.quote: Solvate isomers differ by whether or not a solvent molecule is directly bonded to the metal ion or merely present as free solvent molecules in the crystal lattice.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Give the solvate isomer of the aqua complex [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3 (violet).
cards.back: An example is provided by the aqua complex [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3 (violet) and its solvate isomer [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2.H2O (grey-green).
cards.quote: An example is provided by the aqua complex [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3 (violet) and its solvate isomer [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2.H2O (grey-green).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which basic questions could Werner’s theory not answer?
cards.back:
Why only certain elements possess the remarkable property of forming coordination compounds?
Why the bonds in coordination compounds have directional properties?
Why coordination compounds have characteristic magnetic and optical properties?
cards.quote: (i) Why only certain elements possess the remarkable property of forming coordination compounds? (ii) Why the bonds in coordination compounds have directional properties? (iii) Why coordination compounds have characteristic magnetic and optical properties?

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the theories put forth to explain the nature of bonding in coordination compounds.
cards.back:
Valence Bond Theory (VBT)
Crystal Field Theory (CFT)
Ligand Field Theory (LFT)
Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT)
cards.quote: Many approaches have been put forth to explain the nature of bonding in coordination compounds viz. Valence Bond Theory (VBT), Crystal Field Theory (CFT), Ligand Field Theory (LFT) and Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does the valence bond theory say about the orbitals a metal atom or ion uses under the influence of ligands?
cards.back: According to this theory, the metal atom or ion under the influence of ligands can use its (n-1)d, ns, np or ns, np, nd orbitals for hybridisation to yield a set of equivalent orbitals of definite geometry such as octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar and so on (Table 5.2).
cards.quote: According to this theory, the metal atom or ion under the influence of ligands can use its (n-1)d, ns, np or ns, np, nd orbitals for hybridisation to yield a set of equivalent orbitals of definite geometry such as octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar and so on (Table 5.2).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Oxidation state and electronic configuration of cobalt in the diamagnetic octahedral [Co(NH3)6]3+?
cards.back: In the diamagnetic octahedral complex, [Co(NH3)6]3+, the cobalt ion is in +3 oxidation state and has the electronic configuration 3d6.
cards.quote: In the diamagnetic octahedral complex, [Co(NH3)6]3+, the cobalt ion is in +3 oxidation state and has the electronic configuration 3d6.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is [Co(NH3)6]3+ octahedral and diamagnetic (VBT)?
cards.back: Six pairs of electrons, one from each NH3 molecule, occupy the six hybrid orbitals. Thus, the complex has octahedral geometry and is diamagnetic because of the absence of unpaired electron.
cards.quote: Six pairs of electrons, one from each NH3 molecule, occupy the six hybrid orbitals. Thus, the complex has octahedral geometry and is diamagnetic because of the absence of unpaired electron.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: When is [Co(NH3)6]3+ called an inner orbital (low spin or spin paired) complex?
cards.back: In the formation of this complex, since the inner d orbital (3d) is used in hybridisation, the complex, [Co(NH3)6]3+ is called an inner orbital or low spin or spin paired complex.
cards.quote: In the formation of this complex, since the inner d orbital (3d) is used in hybridisation, the complex, [Co(NH3)6]3+ is called an inner orbital or low spin or spin paired complex.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is the paramagnetic octahedral [CoF6]3– called an outer orbital (high spin or spin free) complex?
cards.back: The paramagnetic octahedral complex, [CoF6]3– uses outer orbital (4d) in hybridisation (sp3d2). It is thus called outer orbital or high spin or spin free complex.
cards.quote: The paramagnetic octahedral complex, [CoF6]3– uses outer orbital (4d) in hybridisation (sp3d2). It is thus called outer orbital or high spin or spin free complex.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is the tetrahedral complex [NiCl4]2– paramagnetic?
cards.back: The compound is paramagnetic since it contains two unpaired electrons.
cards.quote: The compound is paramagnetic since it contains two unpaired electrons.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is [Ni(CO)4] tetrahedral but diamagnetic?
cards.back: Similarly, [Ni(CO)4] has tetrahedral geometry but is diamagnetic since nickel is in zero oxidation state and contains no unpaired electron.
cards.quote: Similarly, [Ni(CO)4] has tetrahedral geometry but is diamagnetic since nickel is in zero oxidation state and contains no unpaired electron.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In the square planar complexes, the hybridisation involved is ____.
cards.back: In the square planar complexes, the hybridisation involved is dsp2.
cards.quote: In the square planar complexes, the hybridisation involved is dsp2.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Square planar complex example: oxidation state and configuration of nickel in [Ni(CN)4]2–?
cards.back: An example is [Ni(CN)4]2–. Here nickel is in +2 oxidation state and has the electronic configuration 3d8.
cards.quote: An example is [Ni(CN)4]2–. Here nickel is in +2 oxidation state and has the electronic configuration 3d8.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is the square planar [Ni(CN)4]2– diamagnetic?
cards.back: Each of the hybridised orbitals receives a pair of electrons from a cyanide ion. The compound is diamagnetic as evident from the absence of unpaired electron.
cards.quote: Each of the hybridised orbitals receives a pair of electrons from a cyanide ion. The compound is diamagnetic as evident from the absence of unpaired electron.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The magnetic moment of coordination compounds can be measured by the ____ experiments.
cards.back: The magnetic moment of coordination compounds can be measured by the magnetic susceptibility experiments.
cards.quote: The magnetic moment of coordination compounds can be measured by the magnetic susceptibility experiments.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why can metal ions with up to three d electrons (Ti3+, V3+, Cr3+) undergo octahedral hybridisation?
cards.back: For metal ions with upto three electrons in the d orbitals, like Ti3+ (d1); V3+ (d2); Cr3+ (d3); two vacant d orbitals are available for octahedral hybridisation with 4s and 4p orbitals.
cards.quote: For metal ions with upto three electrons in the d orbitals, like Ti3+ (d1); V3+ (d2); Cr3+ (d3); two vacant d orbitals are available for octahedral hybridisation with 4s and 4p orbitals.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: For d4, d5 and d6 ions, how many unpaired electrons remain after pairing to vacate two d orbitals?
cards.back: Thus, for d4 (Cr2+, Mn3+), d5 (Mn2+, Fe3+), d6 (Fe2+, Co3+) cases, a vacant pair of d orbitals results only by pairing of 3d electrons which leaves two, one and zero unpaired electrons, respectively.
cards.quote: Thus, for d4 (Cr2+, Mn3+), d5 (Mn2+, Fe3+), d6 (Fe2+, Co3+) cases, a vacant pair of d orbitals results only by pairing of 3d electrons which leaves two, one and zero unpaired electrons, respectively.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Unpaired electrons in [Mn(CN)6]3– and [MnCl6]3–?
cards.back: [Mn(CN)6]3– has magnetic moment of two unpaired electrons while [MnCl6]3– has a paramagnetic moment of four unpaired electrons.
cards.quote: [Mn(CN)6]3– has magnetic moment of two unpaired electrons while [MnCl6]3– has a paramagnetic moment of four unpaired electrons.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Unpaired electrons in [Fe(CN)6]3– and [FeF6]3–?
cards.back: [Fe(CN)6]3– has magnetic moment of a single unpaired electron while [FeF6]3– has a paramagnetic moment of five unpaired electrons.
cards.quote: [Fe(CN)6]3– has magnetic moment of a single unpaired electron while [FeF6]3– has a paramagnetic moment of five unpaired electrons.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Magnetic behaviour of [CoF6]3– and [Co(C2O4)3]3–?
cards.back: [CoF6]3– is paramagnetic with four unpaired electrons while [Co(C2O4)3]3– is diamagnetic.
cards.quote: [CoF6]3– is paramagnetic with four unpaired electrons while [Co(C2O4)3]3– is diamagnetic.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which of [Mn(CN)6]3–, [Fe(CN)6]3–, [Co(C2O4)3]3– are inner orbital complexes, and what is the hybridisation?
cards.back: [Mn(CN)6]3–, [Fe(CN)6]3– and [Co(C2O4)3]3– are inner orbital complexes involving d2sp3 hybridisation, the former two complexes are paramagnetic and the latter diamagnetic.
cards.quote: [Mn(CN)6]3–, [Fe(CN)6]3– and [Co(C2O4)3]3– are inner orbital complexes involving d2sp3 hybridisation, the former two complexes are paramagnetic and the latter diamagnetic.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which of [MnCl6]3–, [FeF6]3–, [CoF6]3– are outer orbital complexes, and what is the hybridisation?
cards.back: On the other hand, [MnCl6]3–, [FeF6]3– and [CoF6]3– are outer orbital complexes involving sp3d2 hybridisation and are paramagnetic corresponding to four, five and four unpaired electrons.
cards.quote: On the other hand, [MnCl6]3–, [FeF6]3– and [CoF6]3– are outer orbital complexes involving sp3d2 hybridisation and are paramagnetic corresponding to four, five and four unpaired electrons.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: [MnBr4]2– has a spin only magnetic moment of 5.9 BM: tetrahedral or square planar, and why?
cards.back: it should be tetrahedral in shape rather than square planar because of the presence of five unpaired electrons in the d orbitals.
cards.quote: it should be tetrahedral in shape rather than square planar because of the presence of five unpaired electrons in the d orbitals.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: State the limitations (shortcomings) of valence bond theory.
cards.back:
It involves a number of assumptions.
It does not give quantitative interpretation of magnetic data.
It does not explain the colour exhibited by coordination compounds.
It does not give a quantitative interpretation of the thermodynamic or kinetic stabilities of coordination compounds.
It does not make exact predictions regarding the tetrahedral and square planar structures of 4-coordinate complexes.
It does not distinguish between weak and strong ligands.
cards.quote: (i) It involves a number of assumptions. (ii) It does not give quantitative interpretation of magnetic data. (iii) It does not explain the colour exhibited by coordination compounds. (iv) It does not give a quantitative interpretation of the thermodynamic or kinetic stabilities of coordination compounds. (v) It does not make exact predictions regarding the tetrahedral and square planar structures of 4-coordinate complexes. (vi) It does not distinguish between weak and strong ligands.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the crystal field theory (CFT)?
cards.back: The crystal field theory (CFT) is an electrostatic model which considers the metal-ligand bond to be ionic arising purely from electrostatic interactions between the metal ion and the ligand.
cards.quote: The crystal field theory (CFT) is an electrostatic model which considers the metal-ligand bond to be ionic arising purely from electrostatic interactions between the metal ion and the ligand.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Ligands are treated as ____ in case of anions or ____ in case of neutral molecules.
cards.back: Ligands are treated as point charges in case of anions or point dipoles in case of neutral molecules.
cards.quote: Ligands are treated as point charges in case of anions or point dipoles in case of neutral molecules.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The five d orbitals in an isolated gaseous metal atom/ion have same energy, i.e., they are ____.
cards.back: The five d orbitals in an isolated gaseous metal atom/ion have same energy, i.e., they are degenerate.
cards.quote: The five d orbitals in an isolated gaseous metal atom/ion have same energy, i.e., they are degenerate.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why are the dx2–y2 and dz2 orbitals raised in energy in an octahedral field?
cards.back: orbitals which point towards the axes along the direction of the ligand will experience more repulsion and will be raised in energy
cards.quote: orbitals which point towards the axes along the direction of the ligand will experience more repulsion and will be raised in energy
cards.note: dx2-y2 and dz2 form the higher-energy eg set.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which d orbitals are lowered in energy in an octahedral crystal field?
cards.back: the dxy, dyz and dxz orbitals which are directed between the axes will be lowered in energy relative to the average energy in the spherical crystal field.
cards.quote: the dxy, dyz and dxz orbitals which are directed between the axes will be lowered in energy relative to the average energy in the spherical crystal field.
cards.note: dxy, dyz and dxz form the lower-energy t2g set.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How does an octahedral field split the five d orbitals?
cards.back: Thus, the degeneracy of the d orbitals has been removed due to ligand electron-metal electron repulsions in the octahedral complex to yield three orbitals of lower energy, t2g set and two orbitals of higher energy, eg set.
cards.quote: Thus, the degeneracy of the d orbitals has been removed due to ligand electron-metal electron repulsions in the octahedral complex to yield three orbitals of lower energy, t2g set and two orbitals of higher energy, eg set.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Octahedral field: by how much does the energy of the two eg orbitals rise and of the three t2g orbitals fall?
cards.back: Thus, the energy of the two eg orbitals will increase by (3/5) Do and that of the three t2g will decrease by (2/5)Do.
cards.quote: Thus, the energy of the two eg orbitals will increase by (3/5) Do and that of the three t2g will decrease by (2/5)Do.
cards.note: Do in the text is Δo, the octahedral crystal field splitting energy.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: On what does the crystal field splitting energy depend?
cards.back: depends upon the field produced by the ligand and charge on the metal ion
cards.quote: depends upon the field produced by the ligand and charge on the metal ion

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Write the spectrochemical series, in the order of increasing field strength.
cards.back: I– < Br– < SCN – < Cl– < S2– < F – < OH– < C2O42– < H2O < NCS– < edta4– < NH3 < en < CN – < CO
cards.quote: In general, ligands can be arranged in a series in the order of increasing field strength as given below: I– < Br– < SCN – < Cl– < S2– < F – < OH– < C2O42– < H2O < NCS– < edta4– < NH3 < en < CN – < CO

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the spectrochemical series and on what is it based?
cards.back: Such a series is termed as spectrochemical series. It is an experimentally determined series based on the absorption of light by complexes with different ligands.
cards.quote: Such a series is termed as spectrochemical series. It is an experimentally determined series based on the absorption of light by complexes with different ligands.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In d2 and d3 octahedral coordination entities, how do the d electrons occupy the orbitals?
cards.back: In d2 and d3 coordination entities, the d electrons occupy the t2g orbitals singly in accordance with the Hund’s rule.
cards.quote: In d2 and d3 coordination entities, the d electrons occupy the t2g orbitals singly in accordance with the Hund’s rule.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: For d4 ions in an octahedral field, which two patterns of electron distribution are possible?
cards.back: (i) the fourth electron could either enter the t2g level and pair with an existing electron, or (ii) it could avoid paying the price of the pairing energy by occupying the eg level.
cards.quote: (i) the fourth electron could either enter the t2g level and pair with an existing electron, or (ii) it could avoid paying the price of the pairing energy by occupying the eg level.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does P (pairing energy) represent in crystal field theory?
cards.back: the pairing energy, P (P represents the energy required for electron pairing in a single orbital)
cards.quote: the pairing energy, P (P represents the energy required for electron pairing in a single orbital)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are weak field ligands? (Do < P)
cards.back: Ligands for which Do < P are known as weak field ligands and form high spin complexes.
cards.quote: Ligands for which Do < P are known as weak field ligands and form high spin complexes.
cards.note: Do in the text is Δo. Weak field: small splitting, so electrons occupy eg before pairing.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are strong field ligands? (Do > P, the fourth electron pairs in t2g)
cards.back: Ligands which produce this effect are known as strong field ligands and form low spin complexes.
cards.quote: Ligands which produce this effect are known as strong field ligands and form low spin complexes.
cards.note: Do in the text is Δo. Strong field: large splitting, so electrons pair in t2g first.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Calculations show that ____ coordination entities are more stable for strong field as compared to weak field cases.
cards.back: Calculations show that d4 to d7 coordination entities are more stable for strong field as compared to weak field cases.
cards.quote: Calculations show that d4 to d7 coordination entities are more stable for strong field as compared to weak field cases.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In tetrahedral coordination entity formation, the d orbital splitting (Fig. 5.9) is ____ and is ____ as compared to the octahedral field splitting.
cards.back: In tetrahedral coordination entity formation, the d orbital splitting (Fig. 5.9) is inverted and is smaller as compared to the octahedral field splitting.
cards.quote: In tetrahedral coordination entity formation, the d orbital splitting (Fig. 5.9) is inverted and is smaller as compared to the octahedral field splitting.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Formula: tetrahedral splitting (Dt) in terms of octahedral splitting (D0), for the same metal and ligands.
cards.quote: For the same metal, the same ligands and metal-ligand distances, it can be shown that Dt = (4/9) D0.
cards.note: D is Δ in the book: Δt = (4/9) Δo.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Consequently, the orbital splitting energies are not sufficiently large for forcing pairing and, therefore, ____ configurations are rarely observed.
cards.back: Consequently, the orbital splitting energies are not sufficiently large for forcing pairing and, therefore, low spin configurations are rarely observed.
cards.quote: Consequently, the orbital splitting energies are not sufficiently large for forcing pairing and, therefore, low spin configurations are rarely observed.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The colour of the complex is ____ to that which is absorbed.
cards.back: The colour of the complex is complementary to that which is absorbed.
cards.quote: The colour of the complex is complementary to that which is absorbed.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: If green light is absorbed by a complex, what colour does it appear?
cards.back: The complementary colour is the colour generated from the wavelength left over; if green light is absorbed by the complex, it appears red.
cards.quote: The complementary colour is the colour generated from the wavelength left over; if green light is absorbed by the complex, it appears red.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: [Ti(H2O)6]3+: which light is absorbed to excite the electron from the t2g level to the eg level?
cards.back: If light corresponding to the energy of blue-green region is absorbed by the complex, it would excite the electron from t2g level to the eg level
cards.quote: If light corresponding to the energy of blue-green region is absorbed by the complex, it would excite the electron from t2g level to the eg level

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The crystal field theory attributes the colour of the coordination compounds to ____ of the electron.
cards.back: The crystal field theory attributes the colour of the coordination compounds to d-d transition of the electron.
cards.quote: The crystal field theory attributes the colour of the coordination compounds to d-d transition of the electron.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Colour of anhydrous CuSO4 and of CuSO4.5H2O?
cards.back: Similarly, anhydrous CuSO4 is white, but CuSO4.5H2O is blue in colour.
cards.quote: Similarly, anhydrous CuSO4 is white, but CuSO4.5H2O is blue in colour.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is ruby, and which ions give it its colour?
cards.back: Ruby [Fig.5.12(a)] is aluminium oxide (Al2O3) containing about 0.5-1% Cr3+ ions (d3), which are randomly distributed in positions normally occupied by Al3+.
cards.quote: Ruby [Fig.5.12(a)] is aluminium oxide (Al2O3) containing about 0.5-1% Cr3+ ions (d3), which are randomly distributed in positions normally occupied by Al3+.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does the crystal field model explain successfully, to a large extent?
cards.back: The crystal field model is successful in explaining the formation, structures, colour and magnetic properties of coordination compounds to a large extent.
cards.quote: The crystal field model is successful in explaining the formation, structures, colour and magnetic properties of coordination compounds to a large extent.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: CFT limitation: what does the point-charge assumption predict for anionic ligands, and what is actually found?
cards.back: However, from the assumptions that the ligands are point charges, it follows that anionic ligands should exert the greatest splitting effect. The anionic ligands actually are found at the low end of the spectrochemical series.
cards.quote: However, from the assumptions that the ligands are point charges, it follows that anionic ligands should exert the greatest splitting effect. The anionic ligands actually are found at the low end of the spectrochemical series.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Further, it does not take into account the ____ of bonding between the ligand and the central atom.
cards.back: Further, it does not take into account the covalent character of bonding between the ligand and the central atom.
cards.quote: Further, it does not take into account the covalent character of bonding between the ligand and the central atom.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are homoleptic carbonyls?
cards.back: The homoleptic carbonyls (compounds containing carbonyl ligands only) are formed by most of the transition metals.
cards.quote: The homoleptic carbonyls (compounds containing carbonyl ligands only) are formed by most of the transition metals.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Shapes of tetracarbonylnickel(0), pentacarbonyliron(0) and hexacarbonylchromium(0)?
cards.back: Tetracarbonylnickel(0) is tetrahedral, pentacarbonyliron(0) is trigonal bipyramidal while hexacarbonyl chromium(0) is octahedral.
cards.quote: Tetracarbonylnickel(0) is tetrahedral, pentacarbonyliron(0) is trigonal bipyramidal while hexacarbonyl chromium(0) is octahedral.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Structures of decacarbonyldimanganese(0) and octacarbonyldicobalt(0)?
cards.back: Decacarbonyldimanganese(0) is made up of two square pyramidal Mn(CO)5 units joined by a Mn – Mn bond. Octacarbonyldicobalt(0) has a Co – Co bond bridged by two CO groups (Fig.5.13).
cards.quote: Decacarbonyldimanganese(0) is made up of two square pyramidal Mn(CO)5 units joined by a Mn – Mn bond. Octacarbonyldicobalt(0) has a Co – Co bond bridged by two CO groups (Fig.5.13).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the areas in which coordination compounds play important functions.
cards.back:
analytical chemistry
metallurgy
biological systems
industry
medicine
cards.quote: These compounds are widely present in the mineral, plant and animal worlds and are known to play many important functions in the area of analytical chemistry, metallurgy, biological systems, industry and medicine.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is the hardness of water estimated?
cards.back: Hardness of water is estimated by simple titration with Na2EDTA. The Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions form stable complexes with EDTA.
cards.quote: Hardness of water is estimated by simple titration with Na2EDTA. The Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions form stable complexes with EDTA.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The selective estimation of these ions can be done due to difference in the ____ of calcium and magnesium complexes.
cards.back: The selective estimation of these ions can be done due to difference in the stability constants of calcium and magnesium complexes.
cards.quote: The selective estimation of these ions can be done due to difference in the stability constants of calcium and magnesium complexes.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Some important extraction processes of metals, like those of ____, make use of complex formation.
cards.back: Some important extraction processes of metals, like those of silver and gold, make use of complex formation.
cards.quote: Some important extraction processes of metals, like those of silver and gold, make use of complex formation.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is gold extracted using complex formation?
cards.back: Gold, for example, combines with cyanide in the presence of oxygen and water to form the coordination entity [Au(CN)2]– in aqueous solution. Gold can be separated in metallic form from this solution by the addition of zinc.
cards.quote: Gold, for example, combines with cyanide in the presence of oxygen and water to form the coordination entity [Au(CN)2]– in aqueous solution. Gold can be separated in metallic form from this solution by the addition of zinc.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How can purification of metals be achieved using coordination compounds?
cards.back: Similarly, purification of metals can be achieved through formation and subsequent decomposition of their coordination compounds.
cards.quote: Similarly, purification of metals can be achieved through formation and subsequent decomposition of their coordination compounds.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is impure nickel purified through a coordination compound?
cards.back: For example, impure nickel is converted to [Ni(CO)4], which is decomposed to yield pure nickel.
cards.quote: For example, impure nickel is converted to [Ni(CO)4], which is decomposed to yield pure nickel.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Chlorophyll, haemoglobin and vitamin B12: the role of each and the metal in it.
cards.back:
The pigment responsible for photosynthesis, chlorophyll, is a coordination compound of magnesium.
Haemoglobin, the red pigment of blood which acts as oxygen carrier is a coordination compound of iron.
Vitamin B12, cyanocobalamine, the anti–pernicious anaemia factor, is a coordination compound of cobalt.
cards.quote: The pigment responsible for photosynthesis, chlorophyll, is a coordination compound of magnesium. Haemoglobin, the red pigment of blood which acts as oxygen carrier is a coordination compound of iron. Vitamin B12, cyanocobalamine, the anti–pernicious anaemia factor, is a coordination compound of cobalt.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name two enzymes with coordinated metal ions that act as catalysts of biological systems (NCERT).
cards.back: Among the other compounds of biological importance with coordinated metal ions are the enzymes like, carboxypeptidase A and carbonic anhydrase (catalysts of biological systems).
cards.quote: Among the other compounds of biological importance with coordinated metal ions are the enzymes like, carboxypeptidase A and carbonic anhydrase (catalysts of biological systems).

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the Wilkinson catalyst used for?
cards.back: Examples include rhodium complex, [(Ph3P)3RhCl], a Wilkinson catalyst, is used for the hydrogenation of alkenes.
cards.quote: Examples include rhodium complex, [(Ph3P)3RhCl], a Wilkinson catalyst, is used for the hydrogenation of alkenes.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which complexes give smooth, even electroplating of silver and gold?
cards.back: Articles can be electroplated with silver and gold much more smoothly and evenly from solutions of the complexes, [Ag(CN)2]– and [Au(CN)2]– than from a solution of simple metal ions.
cards.quote: Articles can be electroplated with silver and gold much more smoothly and evenly from solutions of the complexes, [Ag(CN)2]– and [Au(CN)2]– than from a solution of simple metal ions.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In black and white photography, how is the developed film fixed, and which complex ion forms?
cards.back: In black and white photography, the developed film is fixed by washing with hypo solution which dissolves the undecomposed AgBr to form a complex ion, [Ag(S2O3)2]3–.
cards.quote: In black and white photography, the developed film is fixed by washing with hypo solution which dissolves the undecomposed AgBr to form a complex ion, [Ag(S2O3)2]3–.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which chelating ligands remove excess of copper and iron?
cards.back: Thus, excess of copper and iron are removed by the chelating ligands D–penicillamine and desferrioxime B via the formation of coordination compounds.
cards.quote: Thus, excess of copper and iron are removed by the chelating ligands D–penicillamine and desferrioxime B via the formation of coordination compounds.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is EDTA used for in medicine (NCERT)?
cards.back: EDTA is used in the treatment of lead poisoning.
cards.quote: EDTA is used in the treatment of lead poisoning.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which platinum coordination compounds inhibit the growth of tumours?
cards.back: Some coordination compounds of platinum effectively inhibit the growth of tumours. Examples are: cis–platin and related compounds.
cards.quote: Some coordination compounds of platinum effectively inhibit the growth of tumours. Examples are: cis–platin and related compounds.

source.section: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In modern chemistry, what are Werner’s primary and secondary linkages recognised as?
cards.back: His theory postulated the use of two types of linkages (primary and secondary) by a metal atom/ion in a coordination compound. In the modern language of chemistry these linkages are recognised as the ionisable (ionic) and non-ionisable (covalent) bonds, respectively.
cards.quote: His theory postulated the use of two types of linkages (primary and secondary) by a metal atom/ion in a coordination compound. In the modern language of chemistry these linkages are recognised as the ionisable (ionic) and non-ionisable (covalent) bonds, respectively.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does valence bond theory fail to provide, and what does it not address?
cards.back: It, however, fails to provide a quantitative interpretation of magnetic behaviour and has nothing to say about the optical properties of these compounds.
cards.quote: It, however, fails to provide a quantitative interpretation of magnetic behaviour and has nothing to say about the optical properties of these compounds.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the d-block of the periodic table?
cards.back: The d-block of the periodic table contains the elements of the groups 3-12 in which the d orbitals are progressively filled in each of the four long periods.
cards.quote: The d-block of the periodic table contains the elements of the groups 3-12 in which the d orbitals are progressively filled in each of the four long periods.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the f-block of the periodic table?
cards.back: The f-block consists of elements in which 4 f and 5 f orbitals are progressively filled.
cards.quote: The f-block consists of elements in which 4 f and 5 f orbitals are progressively filled.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the four series of the transition metals.
cards.back:
3d series (Sc to Zn)
4d series (Y to Cd)
5d series (La and Hf to Hg)
6d series which has Ac and elements from Rf to Cn
cards.quote: There are mainly four series of the transition metals, 3d series (Sc to Zn), 4d series (Y to Cd), 5d series (La and Hf to Hg) and 6d series which has Ac and elements from Rf to Cn.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The two series of the inner transition metals; 4f (Ce to Lu) and 5f (Th to Lr) are known as ____ and ____ respectively.
cards.back: The two series of the inner transition metals; 4f (Ce to Lu) and 5f (Th to Lr) are known as lanthanoids and actinoids respectively.
cards.quote: The two series of the inner transition metals; 4f (Ce to Lu) and 5f (Th to Lr) are known as lanthanoids and actinoids respectively.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why was the name 'transition metals' originally given?
cards.back: Originally the name transition metals was derived from the fact that their chemical properties were transitional between those of s and p-block elements.
cards.quote: Originally the name transition metals was derived from the fact that their chemical properties were transitional between those of s and p-block elements.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define transition metals according to IUPAC.
cards.back: Now according to IUPAC, transition metals are defined as metals which have incomplete d subshell either in neutral atom or in their ions.
cards.quote: Now according to IUPAC, transition metals are defined as metals which have incomplete d subshell either in neutral atom or in their ions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why are Zn, Cd and Hg of group 12 not regarded as transition metals?
cards.back: Zinc, cadmium and mercury of group 12 have full d10 configuration in their ground state as well as in their common oxidation states and hence, are not regarded as transition metals.
cards.quote: Zinc, cadmium and mercury of group 12 have full d10 configuration in their ground state as well as in their common oxidation states and hence, are not regarded as transition metals.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What do (n-1) and ns stand for in the general configuration of d-block elements?
cards.back: The (n-1) stands for the inner d orbitals which may have one to ten electrons and the outermost ns orbital may have one or two electrons.
cards.quote: The (n-1) stands for the inner d orbitals which may have one to ten electrons and the outermost ns orbital may have one or two electrons.

source.section: 4.2 Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Cr in the 3d series: which configuration does it have instead of 3d44s2?
cards.back: Cr, which has 3d5 4s1 configuration instead of 3d44s2
cards.quote: Cr, which has 3d5 4s1 configuration instead of 3d44s2

source.section: 4.2 Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Cu in the 3d series: which configuration does it have, not 3d94s2?
cards.back: Similarly in case of Cu, the configuration is 3d104s1 and not 3d94s2.
cards.quote: Similarly in case of Cu, the configuration is 3d104s1 and not 3d94s2.

source.section: 4.2 Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: General formula for the outer-orbital configuration of Zn, Cd, Hg and Cn.
cards.back: The electronic configurations of outer orbitals of Zn, Cd, Hg and Cn are represented by the general formula (n-1)d10ns2.
cards.quote: The electronic configurations of outer orbitals of Zn, Cd, Hg and Cn are represented by the general formula (n-1)d10ns2.

source.section: 4.2 Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the characteristic properties of transition elements with partly filled d orbitals.
cards.back:
display of a variety of oxidation states
formation of coloured ions
entering into complex formation with a variety of ligands
cards.quote: With partly filled d orbitals these elements exhibit certain characteristic properties such as display of a variety of oxidation states, formation of coloured ions and entering into complex formation with a variety of ligands.

source.section: 4.2 Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which shows greater similarity in properties, a horizontal row of transition elements or non-transition elements?
cards.back: There are greater similarities in the properties of the transition elements of a horizontal row in contrast to the non-transition elements.
cards.quote: There are greater similarities in the properties of the transition elements of a horizontal row in contrast to the non-transition elements.

source.section: 4.2 Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the typical metallic properties displayed by nearly all transition elements.
cards.back:
high tensile strength
ductility
malleability
high thermal and electrical conductivity
metallic lustre
cards.quote: Nearly all the transition elements display typical metallic properties such as high tensile strength, ductility, malleability, high thermal and electrical conductivity and metallic lustre.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What accounts for the high melting points of transition metals?
cards.back: The high melting points of these metals are attributed to the involvement of greater number of electrons from (n-1)d in addition to the ns electrons in the interatomic metallic bonding.
cards.quote: The high melting points of these metals are attributed to the involvement of greater number of electrons from (n-1)d in addition to the ns electrons in the interatomic metallic bonding.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do melting points vary across a row of transition metals?
cards.back: In any row the melting points of these metals rise to a maximum at d5 except for anomalous values of Mn and Tc and fall regularly as the atomic number increases.
cards.quote: In any row the melting points of these metals rise to a maximum at d5 except for anomalous values of Mn and Tc and fall regularly as the atomic number increases.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why do enthalpies of atomisation show maxima at about the middle of each series?
cards.back: The maxima at about the middle of each series indicate that one unpaired electron per d orbital is particularly favourable for strong interatomic interaction.
cards.quote: The maxima at about the middle of each series indicate that one unpaired electron per d orbital is particularly favourable for strong interatomic interaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Metals with very high enthalpy of atomisation tend to behave how in their reactions?
cards.back: metals with very high enthalpy of atomisation (i.e., very high boiling point) tend to be noble in their reactions
cards.quote: metals with very high enthalpy of atomisation (i.e., very high boiling point) tend to be noble in their reactions

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do enthalpies of atomisation of the second and third series compare with the first series?
cards.back: the metals of the second and third series have greater enthalpies of atomisation than the corresponding elements of the first series
cards.quote: the metals of the second and third series have greater enthalpies of atomisation than the corresponding elements of the first series

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In general, ions of the same charge in a given series show progressive ____ in radius with increasing atomic number.
cards.back: In general, ions of the same charge in a given series show progressive decrease in radius with increasing atomic number.
cards.quote: In general, ions of the same charge in a given series show progressive decrease in radius with increasing atomic number.

source.section: 4.3.2 Variation in Atomic and Ionic Sizes of Transition Metals

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why does the ionic radius decrease across a transition series?
cards.back: It may be recalled that the shielding effect of a d electron is not that effective, hence the net electrostatic attraction between the nuclear charge and the outermost electron increases and the ionic radius decreases.
cards.quote: It may be recalled that the shielding effect of a d electron is not that effective, hence the net electrostatic attraction between the nuclear charge and the outermost electron increases and the ionic radius decreases.

source.section: 4.3.2 Variation in Atomic and Ionic Sizes of Transition Metals

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do the atomic radii of the 3d, 4d and 5d series compare?
cards.back: The curves in Fig. 4.3 show an increase from the first (3d) to the second (4d) series of the elements but the radii of the third (5d) series are virtually the same as those of the corresponding members of the second series.
cards.quote: The curves in Fig. 4.3 show an increase from the first (3d) to the second (4d) series of the elements but the radii of the third (5d) series are virtually the same as those of the corresponding members of the second series.

source.section: 4.3.2 Variation in Atomic and Ionic Sizes of Transition Metals

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is lanthanoid contraction?
cards.back: The filling of 4f before 5d orbital results in a regular decrease in atomic radii called Lanthanoid contraction which essentially compensates for the expected increase in atomic size with increasing atomic number.
cards.quote: The filling of 4f before 5d orbital results in a regular decrease in atomic radii called Lanthanoid contraction which essentially compensates for the expected increase in atomic size with increasing atomic number.

source.section: 4.3.2 Variation in Atomic and Ionic Sizes of Transition Metals

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the net result of the lanthanoid contraction for the second and third d series?
cards.back: The net result of the lanthanoid contraction is that the second and the third d series exhibit similar radii (e.g., Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm) and have very similar physical and chemical properties much more than that expected on the basis of usual family relationship.
cards.quote: The net result of the lanthanoid contraction is that the second and the third d series exhibit similar radii (e.g., Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm) and have very similar physical and chemical properties much more than that expected on the basis of usual family relationship.

source.section: 4.3.2 Variation in Atomic and Ionic Sizes of Transition Metals

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The decrease in metallic radius coupled with increase in atomic mass results in a general increase in the ____ of these elements.
cards.back: The decrease in metallic radius coupled with increase in atomic mass results in a general increase in the density of these elements.
cards.quote: The decrease in metallic radius coupled with increase in atomic mass results in a general increase in the density of these elements.

source.section: 4.3.2 Variation in Atomic and Ionic Sizes of Transition Metals

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why do the transition elements exhibit higher enthalpies of atomisation?
cards.back: Because of large number of unpaired electrons in their atoms they have stronger interatomic interaction and hence stronger bonding between atoms resulting in higher enthalpies of atomisation.
cards.quote: Because of large number of unpaired electrons in their atoms they have stronger interatomic interaction and hence stronger bonding between atoms resulting in higher enthalpies of atomisation.

source.section: 4.3.2 Variation in Atomic and Ionic Sizes of Transition Metals

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why does ionisation enthalpy increase along each transition series from left to right?
cards.back: There is an increase in ionisation enthalpy along each series of the transition elements from left to right due to an increase in nuclear charge which accompanies the filling of the inner d orbitals.
cards.quote: There is an increase in ionisation enthalpy along each series of the transition elements from left to right due to an increase in nuclear charge which accompanies the filling of the inner d orbitals.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How does the variation in ionisation enthalpy along a transition series compare with a period of non-transition elements?
cards.back: The variation in ionisation enthalpy along a series of transition elements is much less in comparison to the variation along a period of non-transition elements.
cards.quote: The variation in ionisation enthalpy along a series of transition elements is much less in comparison to the variation along a period of non-transition elements.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: When d-block elements form ions, which electrons are lost first, ns or (n - 1) d?
cards.back: when d-block elements form ions, ns electrons are lost before (n - 1) d electrons.
cards.quote: when d-block elements form ions, ns electrons are lost before (n - 1) d electrons.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: For which ions does the trend of steady increase in second and third ionisation enthalpy break?
cards.back: However, the trend of steady increase in second and third ionisation enthalpy breaks for the formation of Mn2+ and Fe3+ respectively.
cards.quote: However, the trend of steady increase in second and third ionisation enthalpy breaks for the formation of Mn2+ and Fe3+ respectively.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The lowest common oxidation state of these metals is ____.
cards.back: The lowest common oxidation state of these metals is +2.
cards.quote: The lowest common oxidation state of these metals is +2.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which oxidation states does manganese exhibit?
cards.back: Manganese, for example, exhibits all the oxidation states from +2 to +7.
cards.quote: Manganese, for example, exhibits all the oxidation states from +2 to +7.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why do the extreme ends of the 3d series show fewer oxidation states?
cards.back: The lesser number of oxidation states at the extreme ends stems from either too few electrons to lose or share (Sc, Ti) or too many d electrons (hence fewer orbitals available in which to share electrons with others) for higher valence (Cu, Zn).
cards.quote: The lesser number of oxidation states at the extreme ends stems from either too few electrons to lose or share (Sc, Ti) or too many d electrons (hence fewer orbitals available in which to share electrons with others) for higher valence (Cu, Zn).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do the oxidation states of a transition element differ from each other?
cards.back: The variability of oxidation states, a characteristic of transition elements, arises out of incomplete filling of d orbitals in such a way that their oxidation states differ from each other by unity
cards.quote: The variability of oxidation states, a characteristic of transition elements, arises out of incomplete filling of d orbitals in such a way that their oxidation states differ from each other by unity

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do oxidation states of non-transition elements normally differ, in contrast with transition elements?
cards.back: This is in contrast with the variability of oxidation states of non transition elements where oxidation states normally differ by a unit of two.
cards.quote: This is in contrast with the variability of oxidation states of non transition elements where oxidation states normally differ by a unit of two.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In the groups of the d-block, which oxidation states are favoured by the heavier members, unlike the p-block?
cards.back: Although in the p-block the lower oxidation states are favoured by the heavier members (due to inert pair effect), the opposite is true in the groups of d-block.
cards.quote: Although in the p-block the lower oxidation states are favoured by the heavier members (due to inert pair effect), the opposite is true in the groups of d-block.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Cr(VI) in dichromate in acidic medium is a strong oxidising agent, whereas which oxides are not?
cards.back: Thus Cr(VI) in the form of dichromate in acidic medium is a strong oxidising agent, whereas MoO3 and WO3 are not.
cards.quote: Thus Cr(VI) in the form of dichromate in acidic medium is a strong oxidising agent, whereas MoO3 and WO3 are not.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is Cu unable to liberate H2 from acids (in terms of energy)?
cards.back: The high energy to transform Cu(s) to Cu2+(aq) is not balanced by its hydration enthalpy.
cards.quote: The high energy to transform Cu(s) to Cu2+(aq) is not balanced by its hydration enthalpy.

source.section: 4.3.5 Trends in the M2+/M Standard Electrode Potentials

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What do the high value for Mn and the low value for Fe in Eo(M3+/M2+) show?
cards.back: The comparatively high value for Mn shows that Mn2+(d5) is particularly stable, whereas comparatively low value for Fe shows the extra stability of Fe3+ (d5).
cards.quote: The comparatively high value for Mn shows that Mn2+(d5) is particularly stable, whereas comparatively low value for Fe shows the extra stability of Fe3+ (d5).

source.section: 4.3.6 Trends in the M3+/M2+ Standard Electrode Potentials

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In which halides are the highest oxidation numbers achieved?
cards.back: The highest oxidation numbers are achieved in TiX4 (tetrahalides), VF5 and CrF6.
cards.quote: The highest oxidation numbers are achieved in TiX4 (tetrahalides), VF5 and CrF6.

source.section: 4.3.7 Trends in Stability of Higher Oxidation States

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is fluorine able to stabilise the highest oxidation state?
cards.back: The ability of fluorine to stabilise the highest oxidation state is due to either higher lattice energy as in the case of CoF3, or higher bond enthalpy terms for the higher covalent compounds, e.g., VF5 and CrF6.
cards.quote: The ability of fluorine to stabilise the highest oxidation state is due to either higher lattice energy as in the case of CoF3, or higher bond enthalpy terms for the higher covalent compounds, e.g., VF5 and CrF6.

source.section: 4.3.7 Trends in Stability of Higher Oxidation States

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What happens to many copper (I) compounds in aqueous solution?
cards.back: However, many copper (I) compounds are unstable in aqueous solution and undergo disproportionation.
cards.quote: However, many copper (I) compounds are unstable in aqueous solution and undergo disproportionation.

source.section: 4.3.7 Trends in Stability of Higher Oxidation States

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In which oxides does the highest oxidation number coincide with the group number?
cards.back: The highest oxidation number in the oxides (Table 4.6) coincides with the group number and is attained in Sc2O3 to Mn2O7.
cards.quote: The highest oxidation number in the oxides (Table 4.6) coincides with the group number and is attained in Sc2O3 to Mn2O7.

source.section: 4.3.7 Trends in Stability of Higher Oxidation States

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which stabilises high oxidation states better, oxygen or fluorine?
cards.back: The ability of oxygen to stabilise these high oxidation states exceeds that of fluorine.
cards.quote: The ability of oxygen to stabilise these high oxidation states exceeds that of fluorine.

source.section: 4.3.7 Trends in Stability of Higher Oxidation States

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the highest Mn fluoride and the highest Mn oxide.
cards.back: Thus the highest Mn fluoride is MnF4 whereas the highest oxide is Mn2O7.
cards.quote: Thus the highest Mn fluoride is MnF4 whereas the highest oxide is Mn2O7.

source.section: 4.3.7 Trends in Stability of Higher Oxidation States

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does it mean that a few transition metals are 'noble'?
cards.back: Many of them are sufficiently electropositive to dissolve in mineral acids, although a few are `noble'--that is, they are unaffected by single acids.
cards.quote: Many of them are sufficiently electropositive to dissolve in mineral acids, although a few are `noble'--that is, they are unaffected by single acids.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which metal of the first series is not oxidised by 1M H+?
cards.back: The metals of the first series with the exception of copper are relatively more reactive and are oxidised by 1M H+, though the actual rate at which these metals react with oxidising agents like hydrogen ion (H+) is sometimes slow.
cards.quote: The metals of the first series with the exception of copper are relatively more reactive and are oxidised by 1M H+, though the actual rate at which these metals react with oxidising agents like hydrogen ion (H+) is sometimes slow.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which M3+ ions are the strongest oxidising agents in aqueous solutions?
cards.back: An examination of the Eo values for the redox couple M3+/M2+ (Table 4.2) shows that Mn3+ and Co3+ ions are the strongest oxidising agents in aqueous solutions.
cards.quote: An examination of the Eo values for the redox couple M3+/M2+ (Table 4.2) shows that Mn3+ and Co3+ ions are the strongest oxidising agents in aqueous solutions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which ions are strong reducing agents that liberate hydrogen from a dilute acid?
cards.back: The ions Ti2+, V2+ and Cr2+ are strong reducing agents and will liberate hydrogen from a dilute acid
cards.quote: The ions Ti2+, V2+ and Cr2+ are strong reducing agents and will liberate hydrogen from a dilute acid

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is the Eo value for the Mn3+/Mn2+ couple much more positive than that for Cr3+/Cr2+ or Fe3+/Fe2+?
cards.back: Much larger third ionisation energy of Mn (where the required change is d5 to d4) is mainly responsible for this. This also explains why the +3 state of Mn is of little importance.
cards.quote: Much larger third ionisation energy of Mn (where the required change is d5 to d4) is mainly responsible for this. This also explains why the +3 state of Mn is of little importance.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do diamagnetic and paramagnetic substances behave in an applied magnetic field?
cards.back: Diamagnetic substances are repelled by the applied field while the paramagnetic substances are attracted.
cards.quote: Diamagnetic substances are repelled by the applied field while the paramagnetic substances are attracted.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are ferromagnetic substances?
cards.back: Substances which are attracted very strongly are said to be ferromagnetic.
cards.quote: Substances which are attracted very strongly are said to be ferromagnetic.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In fact, ferromagnetism is an extreme form of ____.
cards.back: In fact, ferromagnetism is an extreme form of paramagnetism.
cards.quote: In fact, ferromagnetism is an extreme form of paramagnetism.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What gives rise to paramagnetism?
cards.back: Paramagnetism arises from the presence of unpaired electrons, each such electron having a magnetic moment associated with its spin angular momentum and orbital angular momentum.
cards.quote: Paramagnetism arises from the presence of unpaired electrons, each such electron having a magnetic moment associated with its spin angular momentum and orbital angular momentum.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What magnetic moment does a single unpaired electron have?
cards.back: A single unpaired electron has a magnetic moment of 1.73 Bohr magnetons (BM).
cards.quote: A single unpaired electron has a magnetic moment of 1.73 Bohr magnetons (BM).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What causes colour in transition metal ions?
cards.back: When an electron from a lower energy d orbital is excited to a higher energy d orbital, the energy of excitation corresponds to the frequency of light absorbed (Unit 5).
cards.quote: When an electron from a lower energy d orbital is excited to a higher energy d orbital, the energy of excitation corresponds to the frequency of light absorbed (Unit 5).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the colour observed in a transition metal ion?
cards.back: The colour observed corresponds to the complementary colour of the light absorbed.
cards.quote: The colour observed corresponds to the complementary colour of the light absorbed.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are complex compounds?
cards.back: Complex compounds are those in which the metal ions bind a number of anions or neutral molecules giving complex species with characteristic properties.
cards.quote: Complex compounds are those in which the metal ions bind a number of anions or neutral molecules giving complex species with characteristic properties.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why do transition metals form a large number of complex compounds?
cards.back:
comparatively smaller sizes of the metal ions
their high ionic charges
the availability of d orbitals for bond formation
cards.quote: This is due to the comparatively smaller sizes of the metal ions, their high ionic charges and the availability of d orbitals for bond formation.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: To what ability is the catalytic activity of transition metals ascribed?
cards.back: This activity is ascribed to their ability to adopt multiple oxidation states and to form complexes.
cards.quote: This activity is ascribed to their ability to adopt multiple oxidation states and to form complexes.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which ion catalyses the reaction between iodide and persulphate ions?
cards.back: For example, iron(III) catalyses the reaction between iodide and persulphate ions.
cards.quote: For example, iron(III) catalyses the reaction between iodide and persulphate ions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are interstitial compounds?
cards.back: Interstitial compounds are those which are formed when small atoms like H, C or N are trapped inside the crystal lattices of metals.
cards.quote: Interstitial compounds are those which are formed when small atoms like H, C or N are trapped inside the crystal lattices of metals.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the principal characteristics of interstitial compounds.
cards.back:
They have high melting points, higher than those of pure metals.
They are very hard, some borides approach diamond in hardness.
They retain metallic conductivity.
They are chemically inert.
cards.quote: (i) They have high melting points, higher than those of pure metals. (ii) They are very hard, some borides approach diamond in hardness. (iii) They retain metallic conductivity. (iv) They are chemically inert.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is an alloy?
cards.back: An alloy is a blend of metals prepared by mixing the components.
cards.quote: An alloy is a blend of metals prepared by mixing the components.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which metals are used with iron for a variety of steels and stainless steel?
cards.back: The best known are ferrous alloys: chromium, vanadium, tungsten, molybdenum and manganese are used for the production of a variety of steels and stainless steel.
cards.quote: The best known are ferrous alloys: chromium, vanadium, tungsten, molybdenum and manganese are used for the production of a variety of steels and stainless steel.
