cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name two alloys of transition metals with non transition metals.
cards.back: Alloys of transition metals with non transition metals such as brass (copper-zinc) and bronze (copper-tin), are also of considerable industrial importance.
cards.quote: Alloys of transition metals with non transition metals such as brass (copper-zinc) and bronze (copper-tin), are also of considerable industrial importance.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is meant by 'disproportionation' of an oxidation state?
cards.back: When a particular oxidation state becomes less stable relative to other oxidation states, one lower, one higher, it is said to undergo disproportionation.
cards.quote: When a particular oxidation state becomes less stable relative to other oxidation states, one lower, one higher, it is said to undergo disproportionation.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which oxidation state of manganese becomes unstable in acidic solution (example of disproportionation)?
cards.back: manganese (VI) becomes unstable relative to manganese(VII) and manganese (IV) in acidic solution.
cards.quote: manganese (VI) becomes unstable relative to manganese(VII) and manganese (IV) in acidic solution.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which metal does not form an MO oxide, and are MO oxides ionic?
cards.back: All the metals except scandium form MO oxides which are ionic.
cards.quote: All the metals except scandium form MO oxides which are ionic.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: As the oxidation number of a metal increases, ionic character ____.
cards.back: As the oxidation number of a metal increases, ionic character decreases.
cards.quote: As the oxidation number of a metal increases, ionic character decreases.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which chromium oxide is basic and which is amphoteric?
cards.back: The well characterised CrO is basic but Cr2O3 is amphoteric.
cards.quote: The well characterised CrO is basic but Cr2O3 is amphoteric.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are the uses of potassium dichromate?
cards.back: Potassium dichromate is a very important chemical used in leather industry and as an oxidant for preparation of many azo compounds.
cards.quote: Potassium dichromate is a very important chemical used in leather industry and as an oxidant for preparation of many azo compounds.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How are dichromates generally prepared?
cards.back: Dichromates are generally prepared from chromate, which in turn are obtained by the fusion of chromite ore (FeCr2O4) with sodium or potassium carbonate in free access of air.
cards.quote: Dichromates are generally prepared from chromate, which in turn are obtained by the fusion of chromite ore (FeCr2O4) with sodium or potassium carbonate in free access of air.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is potassium dichromate prepared from sodium dichromate?
cards.back: Sodium dichromate is more soluble than potassium dichromate. The latter is therefore, prepared by treating the solution of sodium dichromate with potassium chloride.
cards.quote: Sodium dichromate is more soluble than potassium dichromate. The latter is therefore, prepared by treating the solution of sodium dichromate with potassium chloride.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: On what do the interconversion of chromates and dichromates depend?
cards.back: The chromates and dichromates are interconvertible in aqueous solution depending upon pH of the solution.
cards.quote: The chromates and dichromates are interconvertible in aqueous solution depending upon pH of the solution.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are the structures of chromate and dichromate ions?
cards.back: The chromate ion is tetrahedral whereas the dichromate ion consists of two tetrahedra sharing one corner with Cr–O–Cr bond angle of 126°.
cards.quote: The chromate ion is tetrahedral whereas the dichromate ion consists of two tetrahedra sharing one corner with Cr–O–Cr bond angle of 126°.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does acidified potassium dichromate oxidise?
cards.back: Thus, acidified potassium dichromate will oxidise iodides to iodine, sulphides to sulphur, tin(II) to tin(IV) and iron(II) salts to iron(III).
cards.quote: Thus, acidified potassium dichromate will oxidise iodides to iodine, sulphides to sulphur, tin(II) to tin(IV) and iron(II) salts to iron(III).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is potassium permanganate prepared?
cards.back: Potassium permanganate is prepared by fusion of MnO2 with an alkali metal hydroxide and an oxidising agent like KNO3.
cards.quote: Potassium permanganate is prepared by fusion of MnO2 with an alkali metal hydroxide and an oxidising agent like KNO3.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are the crystals of potassium permanganate like?
cards.back: Potassium permanganate forms dark purple (almost black) crystals which are isostructural with those of KClO4.
cards.quote: Potassium permanganate forms dark purple (almost black) crystals which are isostructural with those of KClO4.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What two physical properties of KMnO4 are of considerable interest?
cards.back: It has two physical properties of considerable interest: its intense colour and its diamagnetism along with temperature-dependent weak paramagnetism.
cards.quote: It has two physical properties of considerable interest: its intense colour and its diamagnetism along with temperature-dependent weak paramagnetism.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the shape of the manganate and permanganate ions?
cards.back: The manganate and permanganate ions are tetrahedral
cards.quote: The manganate and permanganate ions are tetrahedral

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which is paramagnetic and which is diamagnetic, manganate or permanganate?
cards.back: The green manganate is paramagnetic because of one unpaired electron but the permanganate is diamagnetic due to the absence of unpaired electron.
cards.quote: The green manganate is paramagnetic because of one unpaired electron but the permanganate is diamagnetic due to the absence of unpaired electron.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does acidified permanganate solution oxidise?
cards.back: Acidified permanganate solution oxidises oxalates to carbon dioxide, iron(II) to iron(III), nitrites to nitrates and iodides to free iodine.
cards.quote: Acidified permanganate solution oxidises oxalates to carbon dioxide, iron(II) to iron(III), nitrites to nitrates and iodides to free iodine.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is potassium permanganate used as in preparative organic chemistry?
cards.back: Besides its use in analytical chemistry, potassium permanganate is used as a favourite oxidant in preparative organic chemistry.
cards.quote: Besides its use in analytical chemistry, potassium permanganate is used as a favourite oxidant in preparative organic chemistry.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What do the f-block series, lanthanoids and actinoids, consist of?
cards.back: The f-block consists of the two series, lanthanoids (the fourteen elements following lanthanum) and actinoids (the fourteen elements following actinium).
cards.quote: The f-block consists of the two series, lanthanoids (the fourteen elements following lanthanum) and actinoids (the fourteen elements following actinium).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What causes the complication in the chemistry of actinoids?
cards.back: The complication arises partly owing to the occurrence of a wide range of oxidation states in these elements and partly because their radioactivity creates special problems in their study
cards.quote: The complication arises partly owing to the occurrence of a wide range of oxidation states in these elements and partly because their radioactivity creates special problems in their study

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What form do the electronic configurations of all the tripositive lanthanoid ions take?
cards.back: However, the electronic configurations of all the tripositive ions (the most stable oxidation state of all the lanthanoids) are of the form 4f n (n = 1 to 14 with increasing atomic number).
cards.quote: However, the electronic configurations of all the tripositive ions (the most stable oxidation state of all the lanthanoids) are of the form 4f n (n = 1 to 14 with increasing atomic number).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What causes irregularity in oxidation states of lanthanoids?
cards.back: This irregularity (as in ionisation enthalpies) arises mainly from the extra stability of empty, half-filled or filled f subshell.
cards.quote: This irregularity (as in ionisation enthalpies) arises mainly from the extra stability of empty, half-filled or filled f subshell.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which lanthanoid +4 state is favoured by its noble gas configuration, and what is it like?
cards.back: Thus, the formation of CeIV is favoured by its noble gas configuration, but it is a strong oxidant reverting to the common +3 state.
cards.quote: Thus, the formation of CeIV is favoured by its noble gas configuration, but it is a strong oxidant reverting to the common +3 state.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the Eo value for Ce4+/Ce3+, and what does it suggest?
cards.back: The Eo value for Ce4+/ Ce3+ is + 1.74 V which suggests that it can oxidise water.
cards.quote: The Eo value for Ce4+/ Ce3+ is + 1.74 V which suggests that it can oxidise water.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which lanthanoids also exhibit +4 state but only in oxides MO2?
cards.back: Pr, Nd, Tb and Dy also exhibit +4 state but only in oxides, MO2.
cards.quote: Pr, Nd, Tb and Dy also exhibit +4 state but only in oxides, MO2.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which lanthanoid behaves like europium, exhibiting both +2 and +3 states?
cards.back: The behaviour of samarium is very much like europium, exhibiting both +2 and +3 oxidation states.
cards.quote: The behaviour of samarium is very much like europium, exhibiting both +2 and +3 oxidation states.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are the lanthanoids like in appearance and how do they behave in air?
cards.back: All the lanthanoids are silvery white soft metals and tarnish rapidly in air.
cards.quote: All the lanthanoids are silvery white soft metals and tarnish rapidly in air.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which lanthanoid ions are not paramagnetic?
cards.back: The lanthanoid ions other than the f 0 type (La3+ and Ce4+) and the f 14 type (Yb2+ and Lu3+) are all paramagnetic.
cards.quote: The lanthanoid ions other than the f 0 type (La3+ and Ce4+) and the f 14 type (Yb2+ and Lu3+) are all paramagnetic.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How does the chemical behaviour of lanthanoids change with increasing atomic number?
cards.back: In their chemical behaviour, in general, the earlier members of the series are quite reactive similar to calcium but, with increasing atomic number, they behave more like aluminium.
cards.quote: In their chemical behaviour, in general, the earlier members of the series are quite reactive similar to calcium but, with increasing atomic number, they behave more like aluminium.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the best single use of the lanthanoids?
cards.back: The best single use of the lanthanoids is for the production of alloy steels for plates and pipes.
cards.quote: The best single use of the lanthanoids is for the production of alloy steels for plates and pipes.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is mischmetall?
cards.back: A well known alloy is mischmetall which consists of a lanthanoid metal (~ 95%) and iron (~ 5%) and traces of S, C, Ca and Al.
cards.quote: A well known alloy is mischmetall which consists of a lanthanoid metal (~ 95%) and iron (~ 5%) and traces of S, C, Ca and Al.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which elements do the actinoids include?
cards.back: The actinoids include the fourteen elements from Th to Lr.
cards.quote: The actinoids include the fourteen elements from Th to Lr.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is common in the electronic configuration of the actinoids?
cards.back: All the actinoids are believed to have the electronic configuration of 7s2 and variable occupancy of the 5f and 6d subshells.
cards.quote: All the actinoids are believed to have the electronic configuration of 7s2 and variable occupancy of the 5f and 6d subshells.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do 5f orbitals differ from 4f orbitals in bonding?
cards.back: Although the 5f orbitals resemble the 4f orbitals in their angular part of the wave-function, they are not as buried as 4f orbitals and hence 5f electrons can participate in bonding to a far greater extent.
cards.quote: Although the 5f orbitals resemble the 4f orbitals in their angular part of the wave-function, they are not as buried as 4f orbitals and hence 5f electrons can participate in bonding to a far greater extent.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the actinoid contraction?
cards.back: There is a gradual decrease in the size of atoms or M3+ ions across the series. This may be referred to as the actinoid contraction (like lanthanoid contraction).
cards.quote: There is a gradual decrease in the size of atoms or M3+ ions across the series. This may be referred to as the actinoid contraction (like lanthanoid contraction).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is the contraction from element to element greater in actinoids?
cards.back: The contraction is, however, greater from element to element in this series resulting from poor shielding by 5f electrons.
cards.quote: The contraction is, however, greater from element to element in this series resulting from poor shielding by 5f electrons.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why do actinoids show a greater range of oxidation states?
cards.back: There is a greater range of oxidation states, which is in part attributed to the fact that the 5f, 6d and 7s levels are of comparable energies.
cards.quote: There is a greater range of oxidation states, which is in part attributed to the fact that the 5f, 6d and 7s levels are of comparable energies.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which oxidation state do the actinoids show in general?
cards.back: The actinoids show in general +3 oxidation state.
cards.quote: The actinoids show in general +3 oxidation state.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How does the maximum oxidation state change from Th to later actinoids?
cards.back: For example, the maximum oxidation state increases from +4 in Th to +5, +6 and +7 respectively in Pa, U and Np but decreases in succeeding elements (Table 4.11).
cards.quote: For example, the maximum oxidation state increases from +4 in Th to +5, +6 and +7 respectively in Pa, U and Np but decreases in succeeding elements (Table 4.11).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is the lanthanoid contraction more important than the actinoid contraction?
cards.back: The lanthanoid contraction is more important because the chemistry of elements succeeding the actinoids are much less known at the present time.
cards.quote: The lanthanoid contraction is more important because the chemistry of elements succeeding the actinoids are much less known at the present time.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which compound catalyses the oxidation of SO2 in the manufacture of sulphuric acid?
cards.back: V2O5 catalyses the oxidation of SO2 in the manufacture of sulphuric acid.
cards.quote: V2O5 catalyses the oxidation of SO2 in the manufacture of sulphuric acid.

source.section: 4.7 Some Applications of d- and f-Block Elements

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which catalyst is used in the Haber process for ammonia?
cards.back: Iron catalysts are used in the Haber process for the production of ammonia from N2/H2 mixtures.
cards.quote: Iron catalysts are used in the Haber process for the production of ammonia from N2/H2 mixtures.

source.section: 4.7 Some Applications of d- and f-Block Elements

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which catalysts enable the hydrogenation of fats?
cards.back: Nickel catalysts enable the hydrogenation of fats to proceed.
cards.quote: Nickel catalysts enable the hydrogenation of fats to proceed.

source.section: 4.7 Some Applications of d- and f-Block Elements

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which catalyst is used in the Wacker process for the oxidation of ethyne to ethanal?
cards.back: In the Wacker process the oxidation of ethyne to ethanal is catalysed by PdCl2.
cards.quote: In the Wacker process the oxidation of ethyne to ethanal is catalysed by PdCl2.

source.section: 4.7 Some Applications of d- and f-Block Elements

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: On which compound does the photographic industry rely?
cards.back: The photographic industry relies on the special light-sensitive properties of AgBr.
cards.quote: The photographic industry relies on the special light-sensitive properties of AgBr.

source.section: 4.7 Some Applications of d- and f-Block Elements

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which ore is used for the preparation of potassium permanganate?
cards.back: Pyrolusite ore (MnO2) is used for the preparation of potassium permanganate.
cards.quote: Pyrolusite ore (MnO2) is used for the preparation of potassium permanganate.

source.section: 4.7 Some Applications of d- and f-Block Elements

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Silver atom has completely filled d orbitals (4d10) in its ground state. How can you say that it is a transition element?
cards.back: Silver (Z = 47) can exhibit +2 oxidation state wherein it will have incompletely filled d-orbitals (4d), hence a transition element.
cards.quote: Silver (Z = 47) can exhibit +2 oxidation state wherein it will have incompletely filled d-orbitals (4d), hence a transition element.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which of the 3d series of the transition metals exhibits the largest number of oxidation states and why?
cards.back: Manganese (Z = 25), as its atom has the maximum number of unpaired electrons.
cards.quote: Manganese (Z = 25), as its atom has the maximum number of unpaired electrons.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why is the highest oxidation state of a metal exhibited in its oxide or fluoride only?
cards.back: Because of small size and high electronegativity oxygen or fluorine can oxidise the metal to its highest oxidation state.
cards.quote: Because of small size and high electronegativity oxygen or fluorine can oxidise the metal to its highest oxidation state.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define electrochemistry.
cards.back: Electrochemistry is the study of production of electricity from energy released during spontaneous chemical reactions and the use of electrical energy to bring about non-spontaneous chemical transformations.
cards.quote: Electrochemistry is the study of production of electricity from energy released during spontaneous chemical reactions and the use of electrical energy to bring about non-spontaneous chemical transformations.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a galvanic cell?
cards.back: As mentioned earlier a galvanic cell is an electrochemical cell that converts the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy.
cards.quote: As mentioned earlier a galvanic cell is an electrochemical cell that converts the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In the Daniell cell, on which electrode does reduction occur and on which does oxidation occur?
cards.back: The reduction half reaction occurs on the copper electrode while the oxidation half reaction occurs on the zinc electrode.
cards.quote: The reduction half reaction occurs on the copper electrode while the oxidation half reaction occurs on the zinc electrode.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Each half-cell consists of a metallic electrode dipped into an ____.
cards.back: Each half-cell consists of a metallic electrode dipped into an electrolyte.
cards.quote: Each half-cell consists of a metallic electrode dipped into an electrolyte.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The electrolytes of the two half-cells are connected internally through a ____ as shown in Fig. 2.1.
cards.back: The electrolytes of the two half-cells are connected internally through a salt bridge as shown in Fig. 2.1.
cards.quote: The electrolytes of the two half-cells are connected internally through a salt bridge as shown in Fig. 2.1.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: A potential difference develops between the electrode and the electrolyte which is called ____.
cards.back: A potential difference develops between the electrode and the electrolyte which is called electrode potential.
cards.quote: A potential difference develops between the electrode and the electrolyte which is called electrode potential.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define standard electrode potential.
cards.back: When the concentrations of all the species involved in a half-cell is unity then the electrode potential is known as standard electrode potential.
cards.quote: When the concentrations of all the species involved in a half-cell is unity then the electrode potential is known as standard electrode potential.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: According to IUPAC convention, standard reduction potentials are now called ____.
cards.back: According to IUPAC convention, standard reduction potentials are now called standard electrode potentials.
cards.quote: According to IUPAC convention, standard reduction potentials are now called standard electrode potentials.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In a galvanic cell, the half-cell in which oxidation takes place is called ____ and it has a negative potential with respect to the solution.
cards.back: In a galvanic cell, the half-cell in which oxidation takes place is called anode and it has a negative potential with respect to the solution.
cards.quote: In a galvanic cell, the half-cell in which oxidation takes place is called anode and it has a negative potential with respect to the solution.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The other half-cell in which reduction takes place is called ____ and it has a positive potential with respect to the solution.
cards.back: The other half-cell in which reduction takes place is called cathode and it has a positive potential with respect to the solution.
cards.quote: The other half-cell in which reduction takes place is called cathode and it has a positive potential with respect to the solution.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The direction of current flow is ____ to that of electron flow.
cards.back: The direction of current flow is opposite to that of electron flow.
cards.quote: The direction of current flow is opposite to that of electron flow.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define cell potential.
cards.back: The potential difference between the two electrodes of a galvanic cell is called the cell potential and is measured in volts.
cards.quote: The potential difference between the two electrodes of a galvanic cell is called the cell potential and is measured in volts.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is the cell potential related to the electrode potentials of the cathode and anode?
cards.back: The cell potential is the difference between the electrode potentials (reduction potentials) of the cathode and anode.
cards.quote: The cell potential is the difference between the electrode potentials (reduction potentials) of the cathode and anode.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: When is the cell potential called the emf of the cell?
cards.back: It is called the cell electromotive force (emf) of the cell when no current is drawn through the cell.
cards.quote: It is called the cell electromotive force (emf) of the cell when no current is drawn through the cell.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Where is the anode kept when representing a galvanic cell?
cards.back: It is now an accepted convention that we keep the anode on the left and the cathode on the right while representing the galvanic cell.
cards.quote: It is now an accepted convention that we keep the anode on the left and the cathode on the right while representing the galvanic cell.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is a galvanic cell generally represented (the vertical lines)?
cards.back: A galvanic cell is generally represented by putting a vertical line between metal and electrolyte solution and putting a double vertical line between the two electrolytes connected by a salt bridge.
cards.quote: A galvanic cell is generally represented by putting a vertical line between metal and electrolyte solution and putting a double vertical line between the two electrolytes connected by a salt bridge.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Formula: emf of the cell from the right and left half-cell potentials.
cards.back: Under this convention the emf of the cell is positive and is given by the potential of the half-cell on the right hand side minus the potential of the half-cell on the left hand side i.e., Ecell = Eright − Eleft
cards.quote: Under this convention the emf of the cell is positive and is given by the potential of the half-cell on the right hand side minus the potential of the half-cell on the left hand side i.e., Ecell = Eright − Eleft

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What can be measured: the potential of an individual half-cell or only a difference?
cards.back: The potential of individual half-cell cannot be measured. We can measure only the difference between the two half-cell potentials that gives the emf of the cell.
cards.quote: The potential of individual half-cell cannot be measured. We can measure only the difference between the two half-cell potentials that gives the emf of the cell.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The standard hydrogen electrode consists of a platinum electrode coated with ____.
cards.back: The standard hydrogen electrode consists of a platinum electrode coated with platinum black.
cards.quote: The standard hydrogen electrode consists of a platinum electrode coated with platinum black.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What do the unity concentrations of the standard hydrogen electrode imply?
cards.back: This implies that the pressure of hydrogen gas is one bar and the concentration of hydrogen ion in the solution is one molar.
cards.quote: This implies that the pressure of hydrogen gas is one bar and the concentration of hydrogen ion in the solution is one molar.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does the positive standard electrode potential of Cu2+/Cu (0.34 V) indicate?
cards.back: The positive value of the standard electrode potential in the first case indicates that Cu2+ ions get reduced more easily than H+ ions.
cards.quote: The positive value of the standard electrode potential in the first case indicates that Cu2+ ions get reduced more easily than H+ ions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does the negative standard electrode potential of Zn2+/Zn (-0.76 V) indicate?
cards.back: The negative value of the standard electrode potential in the second case indicates that hydrogen ions can oxidise zinc (or zinc can reduce hydrogen ions).
cards.quote: The negative value of the standard electrode potential in the second case indicates that hydrogen ions can oxidise zinc (or zinc can reduce hydrogen ions).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What role do inert electrodes such as platinum or gold play in a half-cell?
cards.back: They do not participate in the reaction but provide their surface for oxidation or reduction reactions and for the conduction of electrons.
cards.quote: They do not participate in the reaction but provide their surface for oxidation or reduction reactions and for the conduction of electrons.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: If the standard electrode potential of an electrode is ____ than zero then its reduced form is more stable compared to hydrogen gas.
cards.back: If the standard electrode potential of an electrode is greater than zero then its reduced form is more stable compared to hydrogen gas.
cards.quote: If the standard electrode potential of an electrode is greater than zero then its reduced form is more stable compared to hydrogen gas.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which is the strongest oxidising agent and which ion the weakest reducing agent in Table 2.1?
cards.back: therefore fluorine gas is the strongest oxidising agent and fluoride ion is the weakest reducing agent.
cards.quote: therefore fluorine gas is the strongest oxidising agent and fluoride ion is the weakest reducing agent.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Lithium has the lowest electrode potential. What does that indicate?
cards.back: Lithium has the lowest electrode potential indicating that lithium ion is the weakest oxidising agent while lithium metal is the most powerful reducing agent in an aqueous solution.
cards.quote: Lithium has the lowest electrode potential indicating that lithium ion is the weakest oxidising agent while lithium metal is the most powerful reducing agent in an aqueous solution.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do oxidising and reducing power change from top to bottom in Table 2.1?
cards.back: It may be seen that as we go from top to bottom in Table 2.1 the standard electrode potential decreases and with this, decreases the oxidising power of the species on the left and increases the reducing power of the species on the right hand side of the reaction.
cards.quote: It may be seen that as we go from top to bottom in Table 2.1 the standard electrode potential decreases and with this, decreases the oxidising power of the species on the left and increases the reducing power of the species on the right hand side of the reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In the Nernst equation, what are the values of R and F?
cards.back: R is gas constant (8.314 JK−1 mol−1), F is Faraday constant (96487 C mol−1), T is temperature in kelvin and [Mn+] is the concentration of the species, Mn+.
cards.quote: R is gas constant (8.314 JK−1 mol−1), F is Faraday constant (96487 C mol−1), T is temperature in kelvin and [Mn+] is the concentration of the species, Mn+.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How does E(cell) of the Daniell cell vary with the concentrations of Cu2+ and Zn2+ ions?
cards.back: It increases with increase in the concentration of Cu2+ ions and decrease in the concentration of Zn2+ ions.
cards.quote: It increases with increase in the concentration of Cu2+ ions and decrease in the concentration of Zn2+ ions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In the Daniell cell, what does zero voltmeter reading with no change in ion concentrations indicate?
cards.back: After some time, we shall note that there is no change in the concentration of Cu2+ and Zn2+ ions and at the same time, voltmeter gives zero reading. This indicates that equilibrium has been attained.
cards.quote: After some time, we shall note that there is no change in the concentration of Cu2+ and Zn2+ ions and at the same time, voltmeter gives zero reading. This indicates that equilibrium has been attained.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How can equilibrium constants that are difficult to measure be obtained?
cards.back: Thus, equilibrium constants of the reaction, difficult to measure otherwise, can be calculated from the corresponding Eo value of the cell.
cards.quote: Thus, equilibrium constants of the reaction, difficult to measure otherwise, can be calculated from the corresponding Eo value of the cell.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The reversible work done by a galvanic cell equals what change in thermodynamic quantity?
cards.back: The reversible work done by a galvanic cell is equal to decrease in its Gibbs energy
cards.quote: The reversible work done by a galvanic cell is equal to decrease in its Gibbs energy

source.section: Electrochemical Cell and Gibbs Energy of the Reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: E(cell) is an ____ parameter
cards.back: E(cell) is an intensive parameter
cards.quote: E(cell) is an intensive parameter

source.section: Electrochemical Cell and Gibbs Energy of the Reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: On what does the electrical resistance of an object depend?
cards.back: The electrical resistance of any object is directly proportional to its length, l, and inversely proportional to its area of cross section, A.
cards.quote: The electrical resistance of any object is directly proportional to its length, l, and inversely proportional to its area of cross section, A.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define resistivity physically.
cards.back: Physically, the resistivity for a substance is its resistance when it is one metre long and its area of cross section is one m2.
cards.quote: Physically, the resistivity for a substance is its resistance when it is one metre long and its area of cross section is one m2.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is conductance?
cards.back: The inverse of resistance, R, is called conductance, G
cards.quote: The inverse of resistance, R, is called conductance, G, and we have the relation:

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the SI unit of conductance?
cards.back: siemens
cards.quote: The SI unit of conductance is siemens

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is conductivity?
cards.back: The inverse of resistivity, called conductivity (specific conductance)
cards.quote: The inverse of resistivity, called conductivity (specific conductance)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does conductivity of a material in S m−1 mean physically?
cards.back: Conductivity of a material in S m−1 is its conductance when it is 1 m long and its area of cross section is 1 m2.
cards.quote: Conductivity of a material in S m−1 is its conductance when it is 1 m long and its area of cross section is 1 m2.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Formula: convert S cm−1 to S m−1.
cards.quote: It may be noted that 1 S cm−1 = 100 S m−1.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Types of materials by magnitude of conductivity.
cards.back:
conductors
insulators
semiconductors
cards.quote: Materials are classified into conductors, insulators and semiconductors depending on the magnitude of their conductivity.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Metals and their alloys have very large conductivity and are known as ____.
cards.back: Metals and their alloys have very large conductivity and are known as conductors.
cards.quote: Metals and their alloys have very large conductivity and are known as conductors.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Substances like glass, ceramics, etc., having very low conductivity are known as ____.
cards.back: Substances like glass, ceramics, etc., having very low conductivity are known as insulators.
cards.quote: Substances like glass, ceramics, etc., having very low conductivity are known as insulators.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Substances like silicon, doped silicon and gallium arsenide having conductivity between conductors and insulators are called ____
cards.back: Substances like silicon, doped silicon and gallium arsenide having conductivity between conductors and insulators are called semiconductors
cards.quote: Substances like silicon, doped silicon and gallium arsenide having conductivity between conductors and insulators are called semiconductors

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Certain materials called ____ by definition have zero resistivity or infinite conductivity.
cards.back: Certain materials called superconductors by definition have zero resistivity or infinite conductivity.
cards.quote: Certain materials called superconductors by definition have zero resistivity or infinite conductivity.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Electrical conductance through metals is called ____ and is due to the movement of electrons.
cards.back: Electrical conductance through metals is called metallic or electronic conductance and is due to the movement of electrons.
cards.quote: Electrical conductance through metals is called metallic or electronic conductance and is due to the movement of electrons.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the factors on which electronic conductance depends.
cards.back:
the nature and structure of the metal
the number of valence electrons per atom
temperature (it decreases with increase of temperature)
cards.quote: The electronic conductance depends on (i) the nature and structure of the metal (ii) the number of valence electrons per atom (iii) temperature (it decreases with increase of temperature).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why does the composition of a metallic conductor remain unchanged during conduction?
cards.back: As the electrons enter at one end and go out through the other end, the composition of the metallic conductor remains unchanged.
cards.quote: As the electrons enter at one end and go out through the other end, the composition of the metallic conductor remains unchanged.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The conductance of electricity by ions present in the solutions is called ____.
cards.back: The conductance of electricity by ions present in the solutions is called electrolytic or ionic conductance.
cards.quote: The conductance of electricity by ions present in the solutions is called electrolytic or ionic conductance.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the factors on which conductivity of electrolytic (ionic) solutions depends.
cards.back:
the nature of the electrolyte added
size of the ions produced and their solvation
the nature of the solvent and its viscosity
concentration of the electrolyte
temperature (it increases with the increase of temperature)
cards.quote: The conductivity of electrolytic (ionic) solutions depends on: (i) the nature of the electrolyte added (ii) size of the ions produced and their solvation (iii) the nature of the solvent and its viscosity (iv) concentration of the electrolyte (v) temperature (it increases with the increase of temperature).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is the first difficulty in measuring the resistance of an ionic solution (DC changes its composition) resolved?
cards.back: The first difficulty is resolved by using an alternating current (AC) source of power.
cards.quote: The first difficulty is resolved by using an alternating current (AC) source of power.

source.section: Measurement of the Conductivity of Ionic Solutions

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is the second problem (a solution cannot be connected to the bridge like a metallic wire) solved?
cards.back: The second problem is solved by using a specially designed vessel called conductivity cell.
cards.quote: The second problem is solved by using a specially designed vessel called conductivity cell.

source.section: Measurement of the Conductivity of Ionic Solutions

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What does a conductivity cell basically consist of?
cards.back: Basically it consists of two platinum electrodes coated with platinum black (finely divided metallic Pt is deposited on the electrodes electrochemically).
cards.quote: Basically it consists of two platinum electrodes coated with platinum black (finely divided metallic Pt is deposited on the electrodes electrochemically).

source.section: Measurement of the Conductivity of Ionic Solutions

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The quantity l/A is called ____ denoted by the symbol, G*.
cards.back: The quantity l/A is called cell constant denoted by the symbol, G*.
cards.quote: The quantity l/A is called cell constant denoted by the symbol, G*.

source.section: Measurement of the Conductivity of Ionic Solutions

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: On what does the cell constant depend, and what is its dimension?
cards.back: It depends on the distance between the electrodes and their area of cross-section and has the dimension of length−1
cards.quote: It depends on the distance between the electrodes and their area of cross-section and has the dimension of length−1

source.section: Measurement of the Conductivity of Ionic Solutions

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is the cell constant usually determined, and with which solutions?
cards.back: The cell constant is usually determined by measuring the resistance of the cell containing a solution whose conductivity is already known. For this purpose, we generally use KCl solutions
cards.quote: The cell constant is usually determined by measuring the resistance of the cell containing a solution whose conductivity is already known. For this purpose, we generally use KCl solutions

source.section: Measurement of the Conductivity of Ionic Solutions

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Conductivity always ____ with decrease in concentration both, for weak and strong electrolytes.
cards.back: Conductivity always decreases with decrease in concentration both, for weak and strong electrolytes.
cards.quote: Conductivity always decreases with decrease in concentration both, for weak and strong electrolytes.

source.section: Variation of Conductivity and Molar Conductivity with Concentration

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why does the conductivity of a solution decrease on dilution?
cards.back: This can be explained by the fact that the number of ions per unit volume that carry the current in a solution decreases on dilution.
cards.quote: This can be explained by the fact that the number of ions per unit volume that carry the current in a solution decreases on dilution.

source.section: Variation of Conductivity and Molar Conductivity with Concentration

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define molar conductivity of a solution at a given concentration.
cards.back: Molar conductivity of a solution at a given concentration is the conductance of the volume V of solution containing one mole of electrolyte kept between two electrodes with area of cross section A and distance of unit length.
cards.quote: Molar conductivity of a solution at a given concentration is the conductance of the volume V of solution containing one mole of electrolyte kept between two electrodes with area of cross section A and distance of unit length.

source.section: Variation of Conductivity and Molar Conductivity with Concentration

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Molar conductivity ____ with decrease in concentration.
cards.back: Molar conductivity increases with decrease in concentration.
cards.quote: Molar conductivity increases with decrease in concentration.

source.section: Variation of Conductivity and Molar Conductivity with Concentration

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Why does molar conductivity increase with decrease in concentration?
cards.back: This is because the total volume, V, of solution containing one mole of electrolyte also increases.
cards.quote: This is because the total volume, V, of solution containing one mole of electrolyte also increases.

source.section: Variation of Conductivity and Molar Conductivity with Concentration

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is limiting molar conductivity?
cards.back: When concentration approaches zero, the molar conductivity is known as limiting molar conductivity
cards.quote: When concentration approaches zero, the molar conductivity is known as limiting molar conductivity

source.section: Variation of Conductivity and Molar Conductivity with Concentration

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the electrolyte types for NaCl, CaCl2 and MgSO4.
cards.back: Thus, NaCl, CaCl2, MgSO4 are known as 1-1, 2-1 and 2-2 electrolytes respectively.
cards.quote: Thus, NaCl, CaCl2, MgSO4 are known as 1-1, 2-1 and 2-2 electrolytes respectively.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: State Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions.
cards.back: The law states that limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte can be represented as the sum of the individual contributions of the anion and cation of the electrolyte.
cards.quote: The law states that limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte can be represented as the sum of the individual contributions of the anion and cation of the electrolyte.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is an electrolytic cell?
cards.back: In an electrolytic cell external source of voltage is used to bring about a chemical reaction.
cards.quote: In an electrolytic cell external source of voltage is used to bring about a chemical reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In an electrolytic cell with copper electrodes in CuSO4, what happens at the anode and the cathode?
cards.back: Thus copper is dissolved (oxidised) at anode and deposited (reduced) at cathode.
cards.quote: Thus copper is dissolved (oxidised) at anode and deposited (reduced) at cathode.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How is impure copper converted into copper of high purity?
cards.back: The impure copper is made an anode that dissolves on passing current and pure copper is deposited at the cathode.
cards.quote: The impure copper is made an anode that dissolves on passing current and pure copper is deposited at the cathode.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How are sodium, magnesium and aluminium produced electrolytically?
cards.back: Sodium and magnesium metals are produced by the electrolysis of their fused chlorides and aluminium is produced by electrolysis of aluminium oxide in presence of cryolite.
cards.quote: Sodium and magnesium metals are produced by the electrolysis of their fused chlorides and aluminium is produced by electrolysis of aluminium oxide in presence of cryolite.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Who was the first scientist to describe the quantitative aspects of electrolysis?
cards.back: Michael Faraday was the first scientist who described the quantitative aspects of electrolysis.
cards.quote: Michael Faraday was the first scientist who described the quantitative aspects of electrolysis.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: State Faraday's first law of electrolysis.
cards.back: First Law: The amount of chemical reaction which occurs at any electrode during electrolysis by a current is proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte (solution or melt).
cards.quote: First Law: The amount of chemical reaction which occurs at any electrode during electrolysis by a current is proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte (solution or melt).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: State Faraday's second law of electrolysis.
cards.back: Second Law: The amounts of different substances liberated by the same quantity of electricity passing through the electrolytic solution are proportional to their chemical equivalent weights (Atomic Mass of Metal ÷ Number of electrons required to reduce the cation).
cards.quote: Second Law: The amounts of different substances liberated by the same quantity of electricity passing through the electrolytic solution are proportional to their chemical equivalent weights (Atomic Mass of Metal ÷ Number of electrons required to reduce the cation).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Formula: quantity of electricity Q passed by a constant current.
cards.back: the quantity of electricity Q, passed is given by Q = It Q is in coloumbs when I is in ampere and t is in second.
cards.quote: the quantity of electricity Q, passed is given by Q = It Q is in coloumbs when I is in ampere and t is in second.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the charge on one electron?
cards.back: We know that charge on one electron is equal to 1.6021 × 10−19C.
cards.quote: We know that charge on one electron is equal to 1.6021 × 10−19C.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Formula: approximate value of 1 F for calculations.
cards.quote: For approximate calculations we use 1F ≈ 96500 C mol−1.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How many moles of electrons reduce one mole of silver ions?
cards.back: One mole of the electron is required for the reduction of one mole of silver ions.
cards.quote: One mole of the electron is required for the reduction of one mole of silver ions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How many Faradays reduce one mole of Mg2+ and one mole of Al3+?
cards.back: It is obvious that one mole of Mg2+ and Al3+ require 2 mol of electrons (2F) and 3 mol of electrons (3F) respectively.
cards.quote: It is obvious that one mole of Mg2+ and Al3+ require 2 mol of electrons (2F) and 3 mol of electrons (3F) respectively.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What charge deposits one mole (63 g) of copper from Cu2+?
cards.back: We require 2F or 2 × 96487 C to deposit 1 mol or 63 g of Cu.
cards.quote: We require 2F or 2 × 96487 C to deposit 1 mol or 63 g of Cu.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What roles do inert and reactive electrodes play in electrolysis?
cards.back: If the electrode is inert (e.g., platinum or gold), it does not participate in the chemical reaction and acts only as source or sink for electrons. On the other hand, if the electrode is reactive, it participates in the electrode reaction.
cards.quote: If the electrode is inert (e.g., platinum or gold), it does not participate in the chemical reaction and acts only as source or sink for electrons. On the other hand, if the electrode is reactive, it participates in the electrode reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: On what do the products of electrolysis depend?
cards.back: The products of electrolysis depend on the different oxidising and reducing species present in the electrolytic cell and their standard electrode potentials.
cards.quote: The products of electrolysis depend on the different oxidising and reducing species present in the electrolytic cell and their standard electrode potentials.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the extra potential called that must be applied for feasible but kinetically slow electrode processes?
cards.back: extra potential (called overpotential) has to be applied
cards.quote: some of the electrochemical processes although feasible, are so slow kinetically that at lower voltages these do not seem to take place and extra potential (called overpotential) has to be applied, which makes such process more difficult to occur.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is any battery basically?
cards.back: Any battery (actually it may have one or more than one cell connected in series) or cell that we use as a source of electrical energy is basically a galvanic cell where the chemical energy of the redox reaction is converted into electrical energy.
cards.quote: Any battery (actually it may have one or more than one cell connected in series) or cell that we use as a source of electrical energy is basically a galvanic cell where the chemical energy of the redox reaction is converted into electrical energy.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What should a battery be like to be of practical use?
cards.back: However, for a battery to be of practical use it should be reasonably light, compact and its voltage should not vary appreciably during its use.
cards.quote: However, for a battery to be of practical use it should be reasonably light, compact and its voltage should not vary appreciably during its use.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In a primary battery, how many times does the reaction occur?
cards.back: In the primary batteries, the reaction occurs only once
cards.quote: In the primary batteries, the reaction occurs only once

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What happens to a primary battery after use over a period of time?
cards.back: over a period of time battery becomes dead and cannot be reused again.
cards.quote: over a period of time battery becomes dead and cannot be reused again.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the most familiar example of a primary battery?
cards.back: The most familiar example of this type is the dry cell (known as Leclanche cell after its discoverer) which is used commonly in our transistors and clocks.
cards.quote: The most familiar example of this type is the dry cell (known as Leclanche cell after its discoverer) which is used commonly in our transistors and clocks.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Describe the electrodes of the dry cell (Leclanche cell).
cards.back: The cell consists of a zinc container that also acts as anode and the cathode is a carbon (graphite) rod surrounded by powdered manganese dioxide and carbon
cards.quote: The cell consists of a zinc container that also acts as anode and the cathode is a carbon (graphite) rod surrounded by powdered manganese dioxide and carbon

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What fills the space between the electrodes of the dry cell?
cards.back: The space between the electrodes is filled by a moist paste of ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) and zinc chloride (ZnCl2).
cards.quote: The space between the electrodes is filled by a moist paste of ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) and zinc chloride (ZnCl2).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the approximate potential of the dry cell?
cards.back: The cell has a potential of nearly 1.5 V.
cards.quote: The cell has a potential of nearly 1.5 V.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is a secondary cell?
cards.back: A secondary cell after use can be recharged by passing current through it in the opposite direction so that it can be used again.
cards.quote: A secondary cell after use can be recharged by passing current through it in the opposite direction so that it can be used again.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which is the most important secondary cell and where is it used?
cards.back: The most important secondary cell is the lead storage battery (Fig. 2.10) commonly used in automobiles and invertors.
cards.quote: The most important secondary cell is the lead storage battery (Fig. 2.10) commonly used in automobiles and invertors.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Describe the electrodes and electrolyte of the lead storage battery.
cards.back: It consists of a lead anode and a grid of lead packed with lead dioxide (PbO2 ) as cathode. A 38% solution of sulphuric acid is used as an electrolyte.
cards.quote: It consists of a lead anode and a grid of lead packed with lead dioxide (PbO2 ) as cathode. A 38% solution of sulphuric acid is used as an electrolyte.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Lead storage battery: anode and cathode reactions when in use.
cards.back:
Anode: Pb(s) + SO42−(aq) → PbSO4(s) + 2e−
Cathode: PbO2(s) + SO42−(aq) + 4H+(aq) + 2e− → PbSO4 (s) + 2H2O (l )
cards.quote: Anode: Pb(s) + SO42−(aq) → PbSO4(s) + 2e− Cathode: PbO2(s) + SO42−(aq) + 4H+(aq) + 2e− → PbSO4 (s) + 2H2O (l )

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Lead storage battery: the overall cell reaction.
cards.back: Pb(s) + PbO2(s) + 2H2SO4(aq) → 2PbSO4(s) + 2H2O(l)
cards.quote: Pb(s) + PbO2(s) + 2H2SO4(aq) → 2PbSO4(s) + 2H2O(l)

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What happens on charging the lead storage battery?
cards.back: On charging the battery the reaction is reversed and PbSO4(s) on anode and cathode is converted into Pb and PbO2, respectively.
cards.quote: On charging the battery the reaction is reversed and PbSO4(s) on anode and cathode is converted into Pb and PbO2, respectively.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What are fuel cells?
cards.back: Galvanic cells that are designed to convert the energy of combustion of fuels like hydrogen, methane, methanol, etc. directly into electrical energy are called fuel cells.
cards.quote: Galvanic cells that are designed to convert the energy of combustion of fuels like hydrogen, methane, methanol, etc. directly into electrical energy are called fuel cells.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is wrong with production of electricity by thermal plants?
cards.back: Production of electricity by thermal plants is not a very efficient method and is a major source of pollution.
cards.quote: Production of electricity by thermal plants is not a very efficient method and is a major source of pollution.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Where was the hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell used for electrical power?
cards.back: The cell was used for providing electrical power in the Apollo space programme.
cards.quote: The cell was used for providing electrical power in the Apollo space programme.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Which catalysts are incorporated into the electrodes of the H2-O2 fuel cell?
cards.back: Catalysts like finely divided platinum or palladium metal are incorporated into the electrodes
cards.quote: Catalysts like finely divided platinum or palladium metal are incorporated into the electrodes

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How long does the fuel cell run?
cards.back: The cell runs continuously as long as the reactants are supplied.
cards.quote: The cell runs continuously as long as the reactants are supplied.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is the efficiency of fuel cells compared to thermal plants?
cards.back: Fuel cells produce electricity with an efficiency of about 70 % compared to thermal plants whose efficiency is about 40%.
cards.quote: Fuel cells produce electricity with an efficiency of about 70 % compared to thermal plants whose efficiency is about 40%.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is corrosion?
cards.back: Corrosion slowly coats the surfaces of metallic objects with oxides or other salts of the metal.
cards.quote: Corrosion slowly coats the surfaces of metallic objects with oxides or other salts of the metal.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Give examples of corrosion.
cards.back: The rusting of iron, tarnishing of silver, development of green coating on copper and bronze are some of the examples of corrosion.
cards.quote: The rusting of iron, tarnishing of silver, development of green coating on copper and bronze are some of the examples of corrosion.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What happens to a metal in corrosion?
cards.back: In corrosion, a metal is oxidised by loss of electrons to oxygen and formation of oxides.
cards.quote: In corrosion, a metal is oxidised by loss of electrons to oxygen and formation of oxides.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Under what conditions does rusting of iron occur?
cards.back: Corrosion of iron (commonly known as rusting) occurs in presence of water and air.
cards.quote: Corrosion of iron (commonly known as rusting) occurs in presence of water and air.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In rusting, where do the electrons released at the anodic spot go?
cards.back: Electrons released at anodic spot move through the metal and go to another spot on the metal and reduce oxygen in the presence of H+
cards.quote: Electrons released at anodic spot move through the metal and go to another spot on the metal and reduce oxygen in the presence of H+

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What is rust chemically?
cards.back: The ferrous ions are further oxidised by atmospheric oxygen to ferric ions which come out as rust in the form of hydrated ferric oxide (Fe2O3. x H2O) and with further production of hydrogen ions.
cards.quote: The ferrous ions are further oxidised by atmospheric oxygen to ferric ions which come out as rust in the form of hydrated ferric oxide (Fe2O3. x H2O) and with further production of hydrogen ions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the methods of preventing corrosion.
cards.back:
covering the surface with paint or by some chemicals (e.g. bisphenol)
cover the surface by other metals (Sn, Zn, etc.)
provide a sacrificial electrode of another metal (like Mg, Zn, etc.)
cards.quote: This can be done by covering the surface with paint or by some chemicals (e.g. bisphenol). Another simple method is to cover the surface by other metals (Sn, Zn, etc.) that are inert or react to save the object. An electrochemical method is to provide a sacrificial electrode of another metal (like Mg, Zn, etc.) which corrodes itself but saves the object.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Galvanic cell vs electrolytic cell: the difference in energy conversion.
cards.back: In galvanic cell, the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction is converted into electrical work, whereas in an electrolytic cell, electrical energy is used to carry out a non-spontaneous redox reaction.
cards.quote: In galvanic cell, the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction is converted into electrical work, whereas in an electrolytic cell, electrical energy is used to carry out a non-spontaneous redox reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How does molar conductivity change on dilution for strong versus weak electrolytes?
cards.back: It increases slowly with decrease in concentration for strong electrolytes while the increase is very steep for weak electrolytes in very dilute solutions.
cards.quote: It increases slowly with decrease in concentration for strong electrolytes while the increase is very steep for weak electrolytes in very dilute solutions.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: With respect to which electrode is standard electrode potential defined?
cards.back: The standard electrode potential for any electrode dipping in an appropriate solution is defined with respect to standard electrode potential of hydrogen electrode taken as zero.
cards.quote: The standard electrode potential for any electrode dipping in an appropriate solution is defined with respect to standard electrode potential of hydrogen electrode taken as zero.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: How do conductivity and molar conductivity change with decrease in concentration?
cards.back: Conductivity decreases but molar conductivity increases with decrease in concentration.
cards.quote: Conductivity decreases but molar conductivity increases with decrease in concentration.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Where do oxidation and reduction of ions take place when ions conduct electricity through a solution?
cards.back: Ions conduct electricity through the solution but oxidation and reduction of the ions take place at the electrodes in an electrochemical cell.
cards.quote: Ions conduct electricity through the solution but oxidation and reduction of the ions take place at the electrodes in an electrochemical cell.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: What results when hydrogen atom(s) of a hydrocarbon are replaced by halogen atom(s)?
cards.back: The replacement of hydrogen atom(s) in an aliphatic or aromatic hydrocarbon by halogen atom(s) results in the formation of alkyl halide (haloalkane) and aryl halide (haloarene), respectively.
cards.quote: The replacement of hydrogen atom(s) in an aliphatic or aromatic hydrocarbon by halogen atom(s) results in the formation of alkyl halide (haloalkane) and aryl halide (haloarene), respectively.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: To which hybridised carbon is halogen attached in haloalkanes, and in haloarenes?
cards.back: Haloalkanes contain halogen atom(s) attached to the sp3 hybridised carbon atom of an alkyl group whereas haloarenes contain halogen atom(s) attached to sp2 hybridised carbon atom(s) of an aryl group.
cards.quote: Haloalkanes contain halogen atom(s) attached to the sp3 hybridised carbon atom of an alkyl group whereas haloarenes contain halogen atom(s) attached to sp2 hybridised carbon atom(s) of an aryl group.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Chlorine containing antibiotic, ____, produced by microorganisms is very effective for the treatment of ____.
cards.back: Chlorine containing antibiotic, chloramphenicol, produced by microorganisms is very effective for the treatment of typhoid fever.
cards.quote: Chlorine containing antibiotic, chloramphenicol, produced by microorganisms is very effective for the treatment of typhoid fever.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Our body produces iodine containing hormone, ____, the deficiency of which causes a disease called ____.
cards.back: Our body produces iodine containing hormone, thyroxine, the deficiency of which causes a disease called goiter.
cards.quote: Our body produces iodine containing hormone, thyroxine, the deficiency of which causes a disease called goiter.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Synthetic halogen compounds, viz. ____ is used for the treatment of malaria; ____ is used as an anaesthetic during surgery.
cards.back: Synthetic halogen compounds, viz. chloroquine is used for the treatment of malaria; halothane is used as an anaesthetic during surgery.
cards.quote: Synthetic halogen compounds, viz. chloroquine is used for the treatment of malaria; halothane is used as an anaesthetic during surgery.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Classify haloalkanes and haloarenes by the number of halogen atoms.
cards.back:
mono
di
polyhalogen (tri-, tetra-, etc.)
cards.quote: These may be classified as mono, di, or polyhalogen (tri-,tetra-, etc.) compounds depending on whether they contain one, two or more halogen atoms in their structures.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define alkyl halides (haloalkanes).
cards.back: In alkyl halides, the halogen atom is bonded to an alkyl group (R).
cards.quote: In alkyl halides, the halogen atom is bonded to an alkyl group (R).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Alkyl halides are classified by the nature of carbon to which halogen is attached. Name the classes.
cards.back:
primary
secondary
tertiary
cards.quote: They are further classified as primary, secondary or tertiary according to the nature of carbon to which halogen is attached.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define allylic halides.
cards.back: These are the compounds in which the halogen atom is bonded to an sp3-hybridised carbon atom adjacent to carbon-carbon double bond (C=C) i.e. to an allylic carbon.
cards.quote: These are the compounds in which the halogen atom is bonded to an sp3-hybridised carbon atom adjacent to carbon-carbon double bond (C=C) i.e. to an allylic carbon.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define benzylic halides.
cards.back: These are the compounds in which the halogen atom is bonded to an sp3-hybridised carbon atom attached to an aromatic ring.
cards.quote: These are the compounds in which the halogen atom is bonded to an sp3-hybridised carbon atom attached to an aromatic ring.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define vinylic halides.
cards.back: These are the compounds in which the halogen atom is bonded to a sp2-hybridised carbon atom of a carbon-carbon double bond (C = C).
cards.quote: These are the compounds in which the halogen atom is bonded to a sp2-hybridised carbon atom of a carbon-carbon double bond (C = C).

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define aryl halides.
cards.back: These are the compounds in which the halogen atom is directly bonded to the sp2-hybridised carbon atom of an aromatic ring.
cards.quote: These are the compounds in which the halogen atom is directly bonded to the sp2-hybridised carbon atom of an aromatic ring.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The ____ of alkyl halides are derived by naming the alkyl group followed by the name of halide.
cards.back: The common names of alkyl halides are derived by naming the alkyl group followed by the name of halide.
cards.quote: The common names of alkyl halides are derived by naming the alkyl group followed by the name of halide.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In the IUPAC system of nomenclature, alkyl halides are named as ____.
cards.back: In the IUPAC system of nomenclature, alkyl halides are named as halosubstituted hydrocarbons.
cards.quote: In the IUPAC system of nomenclature, alkyl halides are named as halosubstituted hydrocarbons.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The dihaloalkanes having the same type of halogen atoms are named as ____.
cards.back: The dihaloalkanes having the same type of halogen atoms are named as alkylidene or alkylene dihalides.
cards.quote: The dihaloalkanes having the same type of halogen atoms are named as alkylidene or alkylene dihalides.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Geminal vs vicinal dihalides: the difference on position of the two halogen atoms.
cards.back: geminal halides or gem-dihalides when both the halogen atoms are present on the same carbon atom of the chain and vicinal halides or vic-dihalides when halogen atoms are present on adjacent carbon atoms.
cards.quote: The dihalo-compounds having both the halogen atoms are further classified as geminal halides or gem-dihalides when both the halogen atoms are present on the same carbon atom of the chain and vicinal halides or vic-dihalides when halogen atoms are present on adjacent carbon atoms.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: In common name system, gem-dihalides are named as ____ and vic-dihalides are named as ____.
cards.back: In common name system, gem-dihalides are named as alkylidene halides and vic-dihalides are named as alkylene dihalides.
cards.quote: In common name system, gem-dihalides are named as alkylidene halides and vic-dihalides are named as alkylene dihalides.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Table 6.1: IUPAC name of chloroform.
cards.back: Trichloromethane
cards.quote: Chloroform Trichloromethane

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Table 6.1: IUPAC name of bromoform.
cards.back: Tribromomethane
cards.quote: Bromoform Tribromomethane

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Table 6.1: IUPAC name of carbon tetrachloride.
cards.back: Tetrachloromethane
cards.quote: Carbon tetrachloride Tetrachloromethane

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Consequently the carbon-halogen ____ also increases from C-F to C-I.
cards.back: Consequently the carbon-halogen bond length also increases from C-F to C-I.
cards.quote: Consequently the carbon-halogen bond length also increases from C-F to C-I.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Alkyl halides are best prepared from ____, which are easily accessible.
cards.back: Alkyl halides are best prepared from alcohols, which are easily accessible.
cards.quote: Alkyl halides are best prepared from alcohols, which are easily accessible.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the reagents that replace the hydroxyl group of an alcohol by halogen.
cards.back:
concentrated halogen acids
phosphorus halides
thionyl chloride
cards.quote: The hydroxyl group of an alcohol is replaced by halogen on reaction with concentrated halogen acids, phosphorus halides or thionyl chloride.

source.section: 6.4 Methods of Preparation of Haloalkanes: 6.4.1 From Alcohols

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: ____ is preferred because in this reaction alkyl halide is formed along with gases SO2 and HCl.
cards.back: Thionyl chloride is preferred because in this reaction alkyl halide is formed along with gases SO2 and HCl.
cards.quote: Thionyl chloride is preferred because in this reaction alkyl halide is formed along with gases SO2 and HCl.

source.section: 6.4 Methods of Preparation of Haloalkanes: 6.4.1 From Alcohols

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The reactions of primary and secondary alcohols with HCl require the presence of a catalyst, ____.
cards.back: The reactions of primary and secondary alcohols with HCl require the presence of a catalyst, ZnCl2.
cards.quote: The reactions of primary and secondary alcohols with HCl require the presence of a catalyst, ZnCl2.

source.section: 6.4 Methods of Preparation of Haloalkanes: 6.4.1 From Alcohols

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Good yields of R-I may be obtained by heating alcohols with sodium or potassium iodide in ____.
cards.back: Good yields of R-I may be obtained by heating alcohols with sodium or potassium iodide in 95% orthophosphoric acid.
cards.quote: Good yields of R-I may be obtained by heating alcohols with sodium or potassium iodide in 95% orthophosphoric acid.

source.section: 6.4 Methods of Preparation of Haloalkanes: 6.4.1 From Alcohols

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Order of reactivity of alcohols with a given haloacid?
cards.quote: The order of reactivity of alcohols with a given haloacid is 3°>2°>1°.

source.section: 6.4 Methods of Preparation of Haloalkanes: 6.4.1 From Alcohols

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Propene yields two products, however only one predominates as per ____.
cards.back: Propene yields two products, however only one predominates as per Markovnikov's rule.
cards.quote: Propene yields two products, however only one predominates as per Markovnikov's rule.

source.section: 6.4 Methods of Preparation of Haloalkanes: 6.4.2 From Hydrocarbons

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Alkyl iodides are often prepared by the reaction of alkyl chlorides/ bromides with NaI in dry acetone. This reaction is known as ____.
cards.back: Alkyl iodides are often prepared by the reaction of alkyl chlorides/ bromides with NaI in dry acetone. This reaction is known as Finkelstein reaction.
cards.quote: Alkyl iodides are often prepared by the reaction of alkyl chlorides/ bromides with NaI in dry acetone. This reaction is known as Finkelstein reaction.

source.section: 6.4 Methods of Preparation of Haloalkanes: 6.4.3 Halogen Exchange

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the metallic fluorides used for the synthesis of alkyl fluorides from alkyl chlorides/bromides.
cards.back:
AgF
Hg2F2
CoF2
SbF3
cards.quote: The synthesis of alkyl fluorides is best accomplished by heating an alkyl chloride/bromide in the presence of a metallic fluoride such as AgF, Hg2F2, CoF2 or SbF3.

source.section: 6.4 Methods of Preparation of Haloalkanes: 6.4.3 Halogen Exchange

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Reactions with iodine are ____ in nature and require the presence of an ____ (HNO3, HIO4) to oxidise the HI formed during iodination.
cards.back: Reactions with iodine are reversible in nature and require the presence of an oxidising agent (HNO3, HIO4) to oxidise the HI formed during iodination.
cards.quote: Reactions with iodine are reversible in nature and require the presence of an oxidising agent (HNO3, HIO4) to oxidise the HI formed during iodination.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: ____ are not prepared by this method due to high reactivity of fluorine.
cards.back: Fluoro compounds are not prepared by this method due to high reactivity of fluorine.
cards.quote: Fluoro compounds are not prepared by this method due to high reactivity of fluorine.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: When a primary aromatic amine, dissolved or suspended in cold aqueous mineral acid, is treated with ____, a ____ is formed.
cards.back: When a primary aromatic amine, dissolved or suspended in cold aqueous mineral acid, is treated with sodium nitrite, a diazonium salt is formed.
cards.quote: When a primary aromatic amine, dissolved or suspended in cold aqueous mineral acid, is treated with sodium nitrite, a diazonium salt is formed.

source.section: 6.5 Preparation of Haloarenes: (ii) From amines by Sandmeyer's reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Mixing the solution of freshly prepared diazonium salt with ____ results in the replacement of the diazonium group by -Cl or -Br.
cards.back: Mixing the solution of freshly prepared diazonium salt with cuprous chloride or cuprous bromide results in the replacement of the diazonium group by -Cl or -Br.
cards.quote: Mixing the solution of freshly prepared diazonium salt with cuprous chloride or cuprous bromide results in the replacement of the diazonium group by -Cl or -Br.

source.section: 6.5 Preparation of Haloarenes: (ii) From amines by Sandmeyer's reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Replacement of the diazonium group by iodine does not require the presence of ____ and is done simply by shaking the diazonium salt with ____.
cards.back: Replacement of the diazonium group by iodine does not require the presence of cuprous halide and is done simply by shaking the diazonium salt with potassium iodide.
cards.quote: Replacement of the diazonium group by iodine does not require the presence of cuprous halide and is done simply by shaking the diazonium salt with potassium iodide.

source.section: 6.5 Preparation of Haloarenes: (ii) From amines by Sandmeyer's reaction

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Alkyl halides are colourless when pure. However, ____ develop colour when exposed to light.
cards.back: Alkyl halides are colourless when pure. However, bromides and iodides develop colour when exposed to light.
cards.quote: Alkyl halides are colourless when pure. However, bromides and iodides develop colour when exposed to light.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Many volatile halogen compounds have ____.
cards.back: Many volatile halogen compounds have sweet smell.
cards.quote: Many volatile halogen compounds have sweet smell.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Methyl chloride, methyl bromide, ethyl chloride and some chlorofluoromethanes are ____ at room temperature.
cards.back: Methyl chloride, methyl bromide, ethyl chloride and some chlorofluoromethanes are gases at room temperature.
cards.quote: Methyl chloride, methyl bromide, ethyl chloride and some chlorofluoromethanes are gases at room temperature.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: That is why the boiling points of ____ are considerably higher than those of the hydrocarbons of comparable molecular mass.
cards.back: That is why the boiling points of chlorides, bromides and iodides are considerably higher than those of the hydrocarbons of comparable molecular mass.
cards.quote: That is why the boiling points of chlorides, bromides and iodides are considerably higher than those of the hydrocarbons of comparable molecular mass.

source.section: 6.6 Physical Properties: Melting and boiling points

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: For the same alkyl group, how do the boiling points of alkyl halides decrease?
cards.back: RI> RBr> RCl> RF
cards.quote: For the same alkyl group, the boiling points of alkyl halides decrease in the order: RI> RBr> RCl> RF.

source.section: 6.6 Physical Properties: Melting and boiling points

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: The boiling points of isomeric haloalkanes decrease with increase in ____.
cards.back: The boiling points of isomeric haloalkanes decrease with increase in branching.
cards.quote: The boiling points of isomeric haloalkanes decrease with increase in branching.

source.section: 6.6 Physical Properties: Melting and boiling points

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Bromo, iodo and polychloro derivatives of hydrocarbons are ____ than water.
cards.back: Bromo, iodo and polychloro derivatives of hydrocarbons are heavier than water.
cards.quote: Bromo, iodo and polychloro derivatives of hydrocarbons are heavier than water.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Name the categories into which the reactions of haloalkanes are divided.
cards.back:
Nucleophilic substitution
Elimination reactions
Reaction with metals
cards.quote: The reactions of haloalkanes may be divided into the following categories: 1. Nucleophilic substitution 2. Elimination reactions 3. Reaction with metals.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: Define nucleophilic substitution reaction.
cards.back: The reaction in which a nucleophile replaces already existing nucleophile in a molecule is called nucleophilic substitution reaction.
cards.quote: The reaction in which a nucleophile replaces already existing nucleophile in a molecule is called nucleophilic substitution reaction.

cards.subject: chemistry
cards.front: A substitution reaction takes place and halogen atom, called ____ departs as halide ion.
cards.back: A substitution reaction takes place and halogen atom, called leaving group departs as halide ion.
